items.title: The coinvariant algebra of a finite Weyl group
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the cited invariant-theory results
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with
Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and Weyl group $W$, acting on $\mathfrak h^*$
by the root reflections of [[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]), hence on the
symmetric algebra $S=S(\mathfrak h^*)$ by graded algebra automorphisms; a nondegenerate $W$-invariant bilinear form identifies $\mathfrak h$
with $\mathfrak h^*$ and thus identifies $S$ with $S(\mathfrak h)$ as
a graded $W$-algebra. Such a form is the complexification of a positive
definite form on the real Cartan, obtained by averaging any positive
definite form over finite $W$. Fix this identification; the page writes
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$ for either presentation. Write
$$S^W_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}(S^W)_d,\qquad I:=S\,S^W_+,$$
so that $I$ is the homogeneous ideal of $S$ generated by the invariants of
positive degree; this is the specialization to the reflection group case of
the quotient construction of
[[def-finite-linear-invariant-and-coinvariant-polynomial-algebras]], because
$S^W_+$ is exactly the space of positive-degree elements of the invariant
algebra $S^W$.

The **coinvariant algebra** of the pair $(\mathfrak h,W)$ is the graded
quotient
$$C=C(\mathfrak h,W):=S/I.$$
It is a commutative graded $\mathbb C$-algebra with $C_0=\mathbb C$: the ideal
$I$ is homogeneous of positive degree, so constants survive and every
homogeneous piece of $S$ maps onto its image. The quotient map
$$\rho:S\longrightarrow C,\qquad \rho(f)=f+I,$$
is a surjective graded algebra homomorphism, and the action of $W$ on $S$
descends to a $\mathbb C$-linear action on $C$ by graded algebra
automorphisms, because $I$ is $W$-stable. The algebra $C$ is finite
dimensional: $W$ is generated by its root reflections, so
[[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]] writes $S$ as a free
module of finite rank over the polynomial algebra $S^W$, and
[[lem-weyl-coinvariant-hilbert-series-has-order-w-dimension]] gives
$\dim_{\mathbb C}C=|W|<\infty$ with the graded Hilbert series recorded there.

**Degree normalization.** Throughout the Soergel material on this page the
Cartan generators are given degree $2$, that is $\deg\mathfrak h=2$; the
symmetric algebra $S$ is then graded with $\deg S_d=2d$ for homogeneous
polynomials of ordinary degree $d$, and $C$ inherits this doubled grading. In
particular a basic invariant of ordinary degree $d_i$ has page degree $2d_i$,
and the top nonzero degree of $C$ is $2N$ with
$N=\sum_i(d_i-1)$. The separate degree-sum lemma on this page proves
that this number equals the positive-root count.

**Auxiliary permutation model for type $A$.** For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_n$
one may instead work with the place-permuting $S_n$-action on the auxiliary
polynomial ring $S_{\mathrm{perm}}=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, where a
permutation $\sigma$ sends $x_i$ to $x_{\sigma(i)}$, and with the quotient
$$C_{\mathrm{perm}}:=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(e_1,\dots,e_n),$$
where $e_1,\dots,e_n$ are the elementary symmetric polynomials. Splitting the
permutation representation $\mathbb C^n=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathbb C\cdot(1,\dots,1)$
into its sum-zero Cartan part and its fixed average coordinate exhibits
$\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]\cong S(\mathfrak h)\otimes\mathbb C[e_1]$ with
$e_1=x_1+\cdots+x_n$ the invariant coordinate, and restriction to the hyperplane
$e_1=0$ has kernel $(e_1)$. By [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-symmetric-polynomials]], $e_1,\dots,e_n$
generate the invariant algebra and its positive-degree ideal of the permutation action, while $e_2,\dots,e_n$ restrict to basic
invariants of $S(\mathfrak h)^W$, dividing out by the positive-degree invariants
commutes with this presentation and yields a canonical isomorphism of graded
algebras
$$C(\mathfrak h,W)\cong C_{\mathrm{perm}}=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(e_1,\dots,e_n),$$
in which $x_i$ has degree $2$ and $e_i$ has degree $2i$. Elements of $C$ are
written as classes $\rho(f)$; the auxiliary model is used only for explicit
rank computations and never replaces the intrinsic definition.

The quotient and finite coordinate constructions require no additional choice;
the freeness and Hilbert-series conclusions inherit AC from their suppliers.
items.strategy: The published definition is quoted for a finite linear group and specialized to the reflection group case; the quotient by the ideal generated by positive-degree invariants is the same construction because $S^W_+$ is the space of invariants of positive degree. Degree normalization is a convention fixed here once for the whole page; For sl_n, split the permutation representation into its sum-zero Cartan and its fixed average coordinate. The fixed coordinate is the invariant e_1/n and is killed in the coinvariant quotient; therefore the auxiliary n-variable quotient by e_1,...,e_n is the Cartan coinvariant algebra, although the unreduced permutation polynomial ring has one extra variable. Products of factors use the corresponding tensor product.

items.title: The regular integral block and its antidominant weight
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block theory
([[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]],
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Work in category $\mathcal O$ of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie
algebra $\mathfrak g$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]]: a Cartan
subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, a positive system with simple roots $\alpha_i$, the
Weyl group $W$ of [[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]], the Weyl
vector $\rho$, and the dot action $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Write
$Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$ and $\mu\le\lambda$ when
$\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$.

**The fixed weight.** Fix a weight $\lambda$ which is **integral**,
**dot-regular** and **dominant**: $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$
for every root $\alpha$ (so the integral Weyl group $W_\lambda$ of
[[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]] is all of $W$), and
$\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$, respectively $>0$, for every
root, respectively every positive root ([[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]]).
The set $\Phi_\lambda$ of [[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]] is therefore
the full root system and $W_\lambda=W$.

**The block.** The regular point $\lambda+\rho$ lies in an open chamber. An element fixing
it preserves that chamber, so [[thm-the-weyl-group-acts-simply-transitively-on-weyl-chambers]]
makes its stabilizer trivial; hence the linkage class
$$C=W_\lambda\cdot\lambda=W\cdot\lambda$$
has exactly $|W|$ elements. The **regular integral block** is the full
subcategory
$$\mathcal O_\lambda:=\mathcal O_C$$
of objects of $\mathcal O$ whose simple composition factors have labels in
$C$, as in [[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]]; it is
nonzero, abelian and extension-closed as a block, and
$K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$ is the subgroup of $K_0(\mathcal O)$ of
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]] spanned by the classes
of objects of the block.

**Its labelled objects.** For $w\in W$ define the standard and costandard
objects and the simple object by
$$\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):=M(w\cdot\lambda),\qquad \nabla(w\cdot\lambda):=D(M(w\cdot\lambda)),\qquad L(w\cdot\lambda):=M(w\cdot\lambda)/J(w\cdot\lambda),$$
where $M$ is the Verma module of [[def-verma-module]], $D$ the restricted dual
of [[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], and $J(w\cdot\lambda)$
the sum of all proper submodules, so that $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ is the unique
simple quotient of $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ by
[[thm-verma-module-has-a-unique-simple-quotient]]. By
[[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]] the simple
objects of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ are exactly the $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ for
$w\in W$, pairwise non-isomorphic. Let $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ denote a projective
cover of $L(w\cdot\lambda)$, which may be chosen inside the linkage class of
$w\cdot\lambda$ and is unique up to isomorphism and indecomposable
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]); every such $P(w\cdot\lambda)$
carries a finite Verma flag
([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]],
[[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]).

**Triangularity of the Verma-flag matrix.** For all $v,w\in W$,
$$[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):L(v\cdot\lambda)]\neq0\ \Longrightarrow\ v\cdot\lambda\le w\cdot\lambda,\qquad [\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]=1,$$
where the multiplicity is the composition multiplicity of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]. Indeed
$(P(v\cdot\lambda):\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))=[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):L(v\cdot\lambda)]$
by [[thm-bgg-reciprocity]] and
$(P(v\cdot\lambda):\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))\neq0$ forces
$w\cdot\lambda-v\cdot\lambda\in Q^+$ while
$(P(v\cdot\lambda):\Delta(v\cdot\lambda))=1$ by
[[cor-projective-standard-labels-lie-above-the-head]].

**The antidominant weight.** Let $w_0\in W$ be the longest element. Since
$\langle w_0\cdot\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle
=\langle\lambda+\rho,w_0^{-1}\alpha^\vee\rangle<0$ for every positive root
$\alpha$, the antidominant Verma module $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ is simple
([[cor-antidominant-verma-modules-are-simple]]), so
$$\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$$
and this is the unique standard object of the block that is simple: for
$w\neq w_0$ the regular weight $w\cdot\lambda$ is not antidominant, so some
positive root $\alpha$ has
$\langle w\cdot\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$, and
[[thm-verma-embedding-for-an-arbitrary-positive-root]] embeds
$M(s_\alpha\cdot(w\cdot\lambda))$ as a proper submodule of
$\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$. The weight $w_0\cdot\lambda$ is called the
**antidominant weight** of the block and $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ its
antidominant Verma module.

**Grothendieck group.** By [[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]
applied to the finite label set $C=W\cdot\lambda$, both the classes
$[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]$ and the classes $[L(w\cdot\lambda)]$, $w\in W$,
form $\mathbb Z$-bases of $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$, and the transition matrix
between them is unitriangular for any linear order of $W$ extending the order
on the dot orbit induced by $\le$.

Every statement above uses the published block, Verma, duality and
projective-cover theory named in the citations, and that theory assumes the
Axiom of Choice; the definition itself selects nothing further.
items.strategy: The block decomposition, linkage classes and the description of central characters are the published items; integrality identifies the integral Weyl group with $W$ and hence the linkage class with the $|W|$-element dot orbit; regularity of $\lambda$ makes its dot-action stabilizer trivial used by the published translation-functor definitions. Indexing of simples and Vermas, the triangularity of the Verma-flag matrix ([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]] with [[cor-projective-standard-labels-lie-above-the-head]], read in the direction $[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):L(v\cdot\lambda)]\neq0\Rightarrow v\cdot\lambda\le w\cdot\lambda$) and the Grothendieck-group bases are the published facts. Every regular integral block has a unique dominant representative in its dot orbit, and that representative is used throughout.

items.title: The sum of basic Weyl invariant degrees minus one counts positive roots
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from invariant theory. Let $\Phi$ be a
finite reduced crystallographic root system of rank $r$ in the real Cartan
space $E$ with Weyl group $W$
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]],
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]), and let
$S=\mathbb C[E]$ carry the induced graded $W$-action with Cartan generators in
ordinary degree $1$. Let $d_1,\dots,d_r$ be the ordinary degrees of basic
invariants, so that $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$ with $w_i$ homogeneous of
degree $d_i$ ([[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]]). Then
$$\sum_{i=1}^r(d_i-1)=|\Phi^+|.$$
With the page degree normalization $\deg E=2$ the coinvariant algebra
$S/(S^W_+S)$ has top degree $2\sum_i(d_i-1)=2|\Phi^+|=|\Phi|$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Molien trace identity: for $|t|<1$, $$\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)=\sum_{d\ge0}\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^W)_dt^d=\frac1{|W|}\sum_{w\in W}\det(1-tw|_E)^{-1}.$$ Indeed the $W$-averaging operator $\pi=(1/|W|)\sum_ww$ is a projection onto $S^W$ in each finite-dimensional degree $S_d$, so $\dim(S^W)_d=\operatorname{tr}\pi|_{S_d}=(1/|W|)\sum_w\operatorname{tr}(w|_{S_d})$; on the other hand, for an operator with eigenvalues $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r$ on $E$, and hence $\mu_1^{-1},\dots,\mu_r^{-1}$ on $E^*$, the degree-$d$ trace $\operatorname{tr}(w|_{S_d})$ is the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial $h_d(\mu_1^{-1},\dots,\mu_r^{-1})$, whose generating function is $\prod_i(1-\mu_i^{-1}t)^{-1}=\det(1-tw^{-1}|_E)^{-1}$; averaging over $w$ and reindexing by $w\mapsto w^{-1}$ gives the displayed formula. [F1, algebra]

1.2 For $w\in W$ let $f$ be the dimension of its fixed space in $E$. Then $\det(1-tw|_E)=(1-t)^fg_w(t)$ with $g_w(t)=\prod_{\lambda\neq1}(1-t\lambda)$ over the remaining eigenvalues $\lambda$ of $w$ and $g_w(1)=\prod_{\lambda\neq1}(1-\lambda)\neq0$; all eigenvalues lie on the unit circle. In particular if $w\neq1$ fixes a hyperplane pointwise, then $f=r-1$, the remaining eigenvalue is $-1$, and $\det(1-tw|_E)=(1-t)^{r-1}(1+t)$. [F4, algebra]

1.3 If $w\in W$, $w\neq1$, fixes a hyperplane $H$ pointwise, then $H=\alpha^\perp$ for some root $\alpha$. Suppose $H$ is different from every root hyperplane. Then all intersections $H\cap\beta^\perp$ are proper linear subspaces of $H$, whose finite union cannot cover it over the infinite field $\mathbb R$ (the product of nonzero defining linear forms is a nonzero polynomial). Thus choose $x\in H$ with $(x,\beta)\neq0$ for every root $\beta$; then $x$ lies in an open chamber $C$, and $w(x)=x$ gives $x\in C\cap w(C)$. As $w$ permutes the chambers, $C\cap w(C)\neq\varnothing$ forces $w(C)=C$, so $w$ lies in the stabilizer of $C$, which is trivial by simple transitivity. Hence $H$ is contained in a root hyperplane, and since both are hyperplanes, $H=\alpha^\perp$ for a root $\alpha$. [F2, F3, choose]

1.4 Put $u=1-t$. Since $1-t^{d_i}=1-(1-u)^{d_i}=d_iu-\frac{d_i(d_i-1)}2u^2+O(u^3)$, one has $(1-t^{d_i})^{-1}=d_i^{-1}u^{-1}(1+\frac{d_i-1}2u+O(u^2))$, and therefore $$\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{d_i})^{-1}=\Bigl(\prod_id_i\Bigr)^{-1}u^{-r}\Bigl(1+\frac{\sum_i(d_i-1)}2u+O(u^2)\Bigr)=\frac1{|W|}u^{-r}\Bigl(1+\frac{\sum_i(d_i-1)}2u+O(u^2)\Bigr),$$ the last equality by [F1]; this product equals $\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)$ for $|t|<1$ by [F1]. [F1, algebra]

2.1 The map $\alpha\mapsto s_\alpha$ induces a bijection from the set $\Phi^+$ of positive roots onto the set of reflections in $W$; consequently $W$ has exactly $|\Phi^+|$ reflections. Injectivity: $s_\alpha=s_\beta$ forces the two reflections to have the same fixed hyperplane, so $\beta=\pm\alpha$, and among positive roots $\beta=\alpha$. Surjectivity: every reflection of $W$ has a fixed hyperplane, which is $\alpha^\perp$ for some root $\alpha$ by step 1.3, and the reflection of $E$ with fixed hyperplane $\alpha^\perp$ is unique, namely $s_\alpha$. Since $s_\alpha=s_{-\alpha}$ and every root hyperplane is $\alpha^\perp$ for exactly one positive root by [F3], distinct positive roots give distinct reflections. [F2, F3, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Expanding the right-hand side of step 1.1 at $t=1$ in the variable $u=1-t$ gives $$\frac1{|W|}\sum_{w\in W}\det(1-tw|_E)^{-1}=\frac1{|W|}\Bigl(u^{-r}+\frac{|\Phi^+|}2u^{-(r-1)}+O(u^{-(r-2)})\Bigr).$$ The identity $w=1$ contributes $u^{-r}$. A nonidentity $w$ with fixed space of dimension $r-1$ is a reflection, and there are exactly $|\Phi^+|$ of them by step 2.1; each contributes $\det(1-tw)^{-1}=(1-t)^{-(r-1)}(1+t)^{-1}=u^{-(r-1)}(\frac12+O(u))$ by step 1.2, because $(1+t)^{-1}=(2-u)^{-1}=\frac12+O(u)$. Every other nonidentity $w$ has $f\le r-2$, hence contributes $u^{-f}\cdot O(1)=O(u^{-(r-2)})$ by step 1.2. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Steps 1.4 and 3.1 compute the same meromorphic function of $u$ near $u=0$; comparing the coefficients of $u^{-(r-1)}$, which are finite, gives $\frac1{|W|}\cdot\frac{\sum_i(d_i-1)}2=\frac1{|W|}\cdot\frac{|\Phi^+|}2$, hence $\sum_i(d_i-1)=|\Phi^+|$. [step 1.4, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 With the page degree normalization $\deg E=2$ the basic invariant $w_i$ has page degree $2d_i$, so the coinvariant algebra has Hilbert series $\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})/(1-t^2)^r$ and its top degree is $\sum_i2d_i-2r=2\sum_i(d_i-1)=2|\Phi^+|=|\Phi|$, by step 4.1 and the published degree computation for the coinvariant algebra. [F1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Adjoint isotypic modules have the zero-weight rank
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra, $S=S(\mathfrak g)$ the symmetric algebra of the adjoint
representation, $R=S^{\mathfrak g}$ its invariants, $Z=Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ the
center of the enveloping algebra, and let $\mathcal H\subseteq S$ be a Kostant
harmonic subspace, so that multiplication is an isomorphism
$R\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H\to S$ of graded $\mathfrak g$-modules with $R$
acting trivially ([[thm-kostant-harmonic-decomposition-of-the-symmetric-algebra]]).

For every finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module $E$ with zero-weight space
$E_0$, the module $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)$ is a free graded
$R$-module of rank $\dim E_0$, and the module
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,U(\mathfrak g))$ is a free $Z$-module of
rank $\dim E_0$; with the filtered lifting $U(\mathfrak g)=Z\cdot\operatorname{sym}(\mathcal H)$
of [[thm-enveloping-algebra-is-free-over-its-center]] these freenesses are
compatible with the natural quotient maps. More precisely,
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)\cong R\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H),\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,U(\mathfrak g))\cong Z\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H),$$
where $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$ is a finite-dimensional
graded vector space of dimension $\dim E_0$; consequently every central
reduction has adjoint $E$-multiplicity $\dim E_0$, and the natural map
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)\otimes_R R/R_+\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S/(R_+S))$
is an isomorphism onto a space of dimension $\dim E_0$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Write $C=S/(R_+S)$ for the coinvariant algebra of the adjoint action. By [F1], $S_d=(R_+S)_d\oplus\mathcal H_d$ in every degree, with both summands $\mathfrak g$-stable; hence the quotient map restricts to an isomorphism $\mathcal H\to C$ of graded $\mathfrak g$-modules, and each $\mathcal H_d$ is finite dimensional. In particular the multiplicity series $H_E(q):=\sum_{d\ge0}\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H_d)q^d$ has nonnegative integer coefficients. [F1]

1.2 By [F2] the ring $R$ is a polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[p_1,\dots,p_r]$ on homogeneous generators $p_i$ of degrees $d_i$, and the Hilbert series $\operatorname{Hilb}(R,q)=\prod_i(1-q^{d_i})^{-1}$ arises from the graded algebra structure of $R$ on $S$. Also $\prod_id_i=|W|$. [F2]

1.3 Since $R$ acts on $S$ by $R$-linear maps commuting with $\mathfrak g$ and acts trivially on $E$, evaluating on $E$ gives an isomorphism of graded $R$-modules $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)\cong R\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$. Indeed $R\otimes\mathcal H$ is free over $R$ on $\mathcal H$ and the adjoint action is $R$-linear, so $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(E,R\otimes\mathcal H)\cong R\otimes\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(E,\mathcal H)$ as $R$-modules and taking $\mathfrak g$-invariants commutes with the graded direct sum. Consequently $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)$ is a free graded $R$-module; it has finite rank exactly when $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$ is finite dimensional, and then its rank is $\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)=H_E(1)$. [F1, algebra]

1.4 The graded character of $S$ is $\operatorname{ch}S=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}(1-qe^{\alpha})^{-1}\cdot(1-q)^{-r}$: the weights of $\mathfrak g$ under the adjoint action are the roots $\alpha\in\Phi$ together with $0$ with multiplicity $r$, and the symmetric algebra on a finite-dimensional module with weights $\mu$ has character $\prod_\mu(1-qe^\mu)^{-1}$ in the completed character ring, the geometric series being interpreted coefficientwise in $\mathbb C[P]\lbrack\lbrack q\rbrack\rbrack$, whose coefficients have finite support. [F4, algebra]

1.5 The simple characters are orthonormal for the constant-term form $$\langle\phi,\psi\rangle=\frac1{|W|}\operatorname{CT}\bigl(\phi\,\psi^{*}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}(1-e^{\alpha})\bigr),\qquad \psi^{*}=\sum_\mu(\dim \psi_\mu)e^{-\mu},$$ where $\operatorname{CT}$ takes the coefficient of $e^0$: by [F4], $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}(1-e^{\alpha})=A(\rho)A(\rho)^{*}$, so the pairing of $\chi_E$ and $\chi_F$ equals $\frac1{|W|}\operatorname{CT}(A(E+\rho)A(F+\rho)^{*})$, and the constant term selects the pairs with $w(E+\rho)=w'(F+\rho)$; each dominant orbit has exactly $|W|$ terms and the signs multiply to $1$, so the value is $\delta_{EF}$. [F4, algebra]

1.6 Realize constant terms as matrix coefficients on $\ell^2(P)$, $P$ the weight lattice, with orthonormal basis $\delta_\mu$: identify $e^\mu$ with $\delta_{-\mu}$ and put $U_\alpha\delta_\mu=\delta_{\mu-\alpha}$, so multiplication by $e^{\alpha}$ corresponds to $U_\alpha$. For $0\le q<1$ the operators $F_\alpha(q)=(I-U_\alpha)(I-qU_\alpha)^{-1}$ are bounded and commute, and $F_{-\alpha}(q)=F_\alpha(q)^{*}$; hence $T(q)=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}F_\alpha(q)=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}F_\alpha(q)F_\alpha(q)^{*}$ is self-adjoint, and $\|F_\alpha(q)\|\le2$ for $q\ge\frac12$: the inverse is the norm-convergent Neumann series $\sum_{n\ge0}q^nU_\alpha^n$, and for every vector $v$, $\|(I-qU_\alpha)v\|^2-q\|(I-U_\alpha)v\|^2=(1-q)^2\|v\|^2\ge0$. Applying this inequality to $(I-qU_\alpha)^{-1}v$ gives $\|F_\alpha(q)\|\le q^{-1/2}\le2$. Moreover $(F_\alpha(q)-I)\delta_0=-(1-q)\sum_{n\ge0}q^n\delta_{-(n+1)\alpha}$ has squared norm $\frac{1-q}{1+q}\to0$, so expanding $\prod_\alpha F_\alpha(q)-I$ as a telescoping sum with one factor $F_\alpha(q)-I$ per term and all other factors bounded by $2$ gives $\|T(q)\delta_0-\delta_0\|\to0$ as $q\to1^{-}$. [F1, construct]

1.7 By [F3] each finite-dimensional $\mathcal H_d$ decomposes into isotypic components, so $\operatorname{ch}\mathcal H=\sum_E H_E(q)\chi_E$ in the completed character ring, the sum over isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak g$-modules; both sides are formal power series whose coefficients are finite characters. [F3, F4]

2.1 Since $R$ has trivial $\mathfrak g$-action, the decomposition $S=R\otimes\mathcal H$ of [F1] tensors characters: $\operatorname{ch}S=\operatorname{Hilb}(R,q)\cdot\operatorname{ch}\mathcal H$. Combining with steps 1.2, 1.4 and 1.7, $$\operatorname{ch}\mathcal H=\prod_i[d_i]_q\cdot\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}(1-qe^{\alpha})^{-1},\qquad [d_i]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{d_i-1}.$$ [F1, step 1.2, step 1.4, step 1.7, algebra]

2.2 Interpreting a finitely supported character as the finite combination of shifts $\psi\mapsto\sum_\mu\psi_\mu U_\mu$ identifies the constant term of step 1.6 with a matrix coefficient: $$\operatorname{CT}\Bigl(\psi\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}\frac{1-e^{\alpha}}{1-qe^{\alpha}}\Bigr)=\langle\psi\,T(q)\delta_0,\delta_0\rangle.$$ [step 1.6, algebra]

3.1 Applying the orthonormality of step 1.5 to the expansion 2.1 gives, for each finite-dimensional simple $E$, with $\chi_E^{*}$ as in step 1.5 and the matrix-coefficient form of step 2.2, $$H_E(q)=\prod_i[d_i]_q\cdot\frac1{|W|}\langle\chi_E^{*}T(q)\delta_0,\delta_0\rangle.$$ This identity is coefficientwise in $q$; for $|q|<1$ the finitely many Neumann series converge in operator norm, so the constant-term power series also converges to the displayed matrix coefficient. [step 1.5, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Letting $q\to1^{-}$ in step 3.1, the matrix coefficient tends to $\langle\chi_E^{*}\delta_0,\delta_0\rangle=\dim E_0$ by the second part of step 1.6, and $\prod_i[d_i]_q\to\prod_id_i=|W|$ by step 1.2; hence $\lim_{q\to1^{-}}H_E(q)=\dim E_0$. [step 1.2, step 1.6, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The coefficients $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H_d)$ of $H_E(q)$ are nonnegative integers and $H_E(q)$ is increasing for $0\le q<1$; the finite limit $\dim E_0$ of step 4.1 therefore forces $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H_d)=0$ for all but finitely many $d$ and $\sum_d\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H_d)=\dim E_0$. Hence $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$ is finite dimensional of dimension $\dim E_0$, and by step 1.3 the module $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)$ is a finitely generated graded free $R$-module of rank $\dim E_0$. [step 1.3, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The identification of step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,C)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$ as graded vector spaces, so $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,C)=\dim E_0$; tensoring the isomorphism of step 1.3 with $R/R_+=\mathbb C$ and using $S\otimes_R(R/R_+)=C$ shows that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)\otimes_R(R/R_+)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,C)$ is an isomorphism. This is the asserted compatibility with the natural quotient map $S\to C=S/(R_+S)$. [step 1.1, step 1.3, step 5.1]

6.2 By [F5] the symmetrization $\operatorname{sym}$ is filtered, $\mathfrak g$-equivariant with associated graded the identity, and the symmetrized lifts of a homogeneous basis of $\mathcal H$ form a $Z$-basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$; thus $U(\mathfrak g)=Z\cdot\operatorname{sym}(\mathcal H)\cong Z\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{sym}(\mathcal H)$ with $Z$ acting trivially under the adjoint action. Applying the argument of step 1.3 with $Z$ in place of $R$ and $\operatorname{sym}(\mathcal H)$ in place of $\mathcal H$ gives an isomorphism of $Z$-modules $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,U(\mathfrak g))\cong Z\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$; by step 5.1 this is a free $Z$-module of rank $\dim E_0$. [F5, step 1.3, step 5.1]

7.1 For every central character with kernel $\mathfrak m\subseteq Z$ the reduction satisfies $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_ZZ/\mathfrak m)\cong(Z/\mathfrak m)\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$, of dimension $\dim E_0$ over $Z/\mathfrak m$; in the polynomial family the reductions $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)\otimes_RR/\mathfrak m$ have the same rank $\dim E_0$, and the special case $\mathfrak m=R_+$, with $S\otimes_R(R/R_+)=C$, is step 6.1. Hence every central reduction has adjoint $E$-multiplicity $\dim E_0$. [step 6.1, step 6.2, algebra]

8.1 For later use we record that the argument also applies to a finite direct sum: if $E=\bigoplus_jE_j$ is a finite direct sum of finite-dimensional modules, then $E_0=\bigoplus_j(E_j)_0$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,-)\cong\bigoplus_j\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E_j,-)$, so all ranks add and the conclusions hold with $\dim E_0=\sum_j\dim(E_j)_0$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from [F1], [F2] and [F5], namely from the Kostant decomposition, the Chevalley restriction and the free-over-center theorem; the multiplicity computation itself uses only finite-dimensional linear algebra, finite sums over the finite Weyl group and single root-lattice shifts. [F1, F2, F5, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Projective functors on a regular integral block
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block theory
([[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Fix a regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$ as in
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]], with
inclusion $\operatorname{incl}_\lambda:\mathcal O_\lambda\to\mathcal O$ and
exact projection $\operatorname{pr}_\lambda:\mathcal O\to\mathcal O_\lambda$
of [[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], so that
$\operatorname{pr}_\lambda\circ\operatorname{incl}_\lambda=\operatorname{id}$;
the block is a direct summand of $\mathcal O$ and contains the projective
covers $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ of [[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]. For a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module $E$ define
the endofunctor
$$F_E:=\operatorname{pr}_\lambda\circ(E\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_\lambda\colon\mathcal O_\lambda\longrightarrow\mathcal O_\lambda .$$

**Basic properties.** The functor $F_E$ is well defined and additive:
$E\otimes-$ is an exact endofunctor of $\mathcal O$ and maps $\mathcal O$ into
itself ([[prop-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-category-o]]),
and $\operatorname{pr}_\lambda$ is exact. Hence $F_E$ is exact as a composite of
exact functors. It preserves projective objects: if $P\in\mathcal O_\lambda$ is
projective, then $E\otimes P$ is projective in $\mathcal O$
([[lem-tensoring-a-projective-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-is-projective]]),
and $\operatorname{pr}_\lambda$ preserves projectives
([[lem-block-projection-preserves-projectives]]). The zero module $E=0$
gives the zero functor, and $E=\mathbb C$ the identity functor, since the
one-dimensional trivial module acts by the identity.

**Projective functors.** A **projective functor** on
$\mathcal O_\lambda$ is an endofunctor of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ isomorphic to a
direct summand of some $F_E$, $E$ finite dimensional and
$\mathfrak h$-semisimple. Write $\mathcal F_\lambda$ for the full subcategory
of the endofunctor category of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ whose objects are the
projective functors, with arbitrary natural transformations as morphisms; it is
additive with the pointwise biproducts of [[def-additive-category]], and
"direct summand" means natural maps $i:F\to F_E$, $p:F_E\to F$ with $pi=1_F$;
then $ip$ is an idempotent natural transformation.

**Closure properties.** The class of projective functors is closed under
finite direct sums, composition, direct summands and passage to adjoints:

1. $F_{E\oplus E'}\cong F_E\oplus F_{E'}$, since tensoring with a direct sum
distributes over direct sums and $\operatorname{pr}_\lambda$ is additive.
2. $F_E\circ F_{E'}$ is a natural direct summand of $F_{E\otimes E'}$:
the natural block decomposition of $E'\otimes X$ splits off its
$\lambda$-component before applying $E\otimes-$ and the final projection.
Its complementary blocks can return to $\mathcal O_\lambda$, so an
isomorphism with the entire $F_{E\otimes E'}$ is not asserted.
3. $F_{E^*}$ is both a left and a right adjoint of $F_E$: this is
[[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]] applied to
the two generalized central characters of the block, since
$F_{E^*}=\operatorname{pr}_\lambda\circ(E^*\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_\lambda$
is the translation functor $T_{\chi_\lambda,E^*,\chi_\lambda}$ and similarly for
$F_E$.
4. A direct summand of an exact additive functor is exact, and a direct summand
of a functor preserving projective objects again preserves projective objects:
apply the splitting to the image of each object. Hence every projective functor
is exact and preserves projective objects, and composition of summand splittings makes a composite of projective
functors a summand of the composite of their ambient tensor functors. Clause 2
therefore proves closure under composition; clause 1 proves closure under sums.
For an adjoint, take the mate of the summand idempotent under clause 3; the
triangle identities carry its square to itself, and its image is the
corresponding adjoint summand of $F_{E^*}$.

This is the definition of Bernstein-Gelfand [BGe, Section 3.1] and of
[Soe90, Section 1.2]; unlike the functors $T_\lambda^\mu$ of
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], projective functors are not
required to come from a single finite-dimensional tensor functor, only from a
direct summand of one.
items.strategy: All closure properties are inherited from the published tensor and block-projection items: exactness and preservation of projective objects, additivity, and the adjunction for $E^*\otimes-$; direct summands of exact functors are exact after splitting, and the idempotent-completion convention for additive categories is [[def-additive-category]]. The composition identity is the associativity of the tensor product of finite-dimensional modules. No choice is used beyond the inherited AC of the block theory.

items.title: The coinvariant algebra is a complete intersection with one-dimensional socle
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published invariant-theory
items. Let $W$ act on the Cartan space $\mathfrak h$ by reflections and on
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$ by graded algebra automorphisms, with coinvariant algebra
$C=S/I$ as in [[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]]. Let
$w_1,\dots,w_r$ be homogeneous basic invariants of page degrees
$2d_1,\dots,2d_r$, where $d_1,\dots,d_r$ are the classical degrees
($\deg\mathfrak h=1$; for the Cartan of $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ they are
$2,3,\dots,n$), so that $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$
([[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]]), and let
$\rho:S\to C$ be the quotient by the ideal $I=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$. Put
$N:=\sum_{i=1}^r(d_i-1)$. Then:

1. The sequence $w_1,\dots,w_r$ is a homogeneous $S$-regular sequence and $C$
is a complete intersection: $C=S/(w_1,\dots,w_r)$ with
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\frac{\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})}{(1-t^2)^r}=\prod_i(1+t^2+\cdots+t^{2(d_i-1)}),$$
so that $\dim_{\mathbb C}C_{2N}=1$ and $C_j=0$ for $j>2N$.
2. The multiplication pairing $C_i\times C_{2N-i}\to C_{2N}\cong\mathbb C$ is
nondegenerate for every $i$, and consequently
$$\operatorname{soc}(C)=\{c\in C:C_+c=0\}=C_{2N}$$ is one dimensional.
3. Equivalently, $C$ is a graded Gorenstein algebra with one-dimensional socle
in the top degree $2N$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The invariant ideal is generated by the basic invariants: $I=S\,S^W_+=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$, because $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$ and every element of $S^W_+$ is a polynomial in the $w_i$ with zero constant term. Hence $C=S/(w_1,\dots,w_r)$; since $C$ is generated by the images of the degree-two elements, its augmentation ideal satisfies $C_+=(x_1,\dots,x_r)C$. [F1]

1.2 The $r$ basic invariants form an $S$-regular sequence: they are minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I$ (they generate $I$, and no $w_i$ lies in the ideal generated by the others, since applying the $S^W$-linear Reynolds projection to a relation in $S$ would give a relation in $\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$, where no variable belongs to the ideal generated by the others), and by [F2] the minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I$ are $r$ in number with common zero set $\{0\}$ and form an $S$-regular sequence; consequently, by [F3], $K(\mathbf w;S)$ is a finite free resolution of $C$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.3 The variables $x_1,\dots,x_r$ form an $S$-regular sequence with $S/(x_1,\dots,x_r)=\mathbb C=:k$, by [F5]; consequently, by [F3], $K(\mathbf x;S)$ is a finite free resolution of $k$. [F3, F5]

1.4 Koszul differentials vanish after base change to $k$: tensoring $K(\mathbf w;S)$ with $k$ multiplies by the images of the $w_i$ in $k$, which lie in the positive-degree part and hence act as zero; so $H_r(K(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk)=K_r(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk$, a one-dimensional space in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 First computation: by resolution 1.2, resolving the $C$ variable, and the balance isomorphism [F6], $\operatorname{Tor}^S_r(C,k)\cong H_r(K(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk)$, which by step 1.4 is one dimensional and concentrated in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$. [F3, F6, step 1.2, step 1.4]

2.2 Second computation: by resolution 1.3, resolving the $k$ variable, and [F6], $\operatorname{Tor}^S_r(C,k)\cong H_r(C\otimes_SK(\mathbf x;S))=H_r(K(\mathbf x;C))$; by [F3] the top homology is $\{c\in C:x_ic=0\text{ for all }i\}$, placed in internal degree $2r$ above the degrees of its elements, since $e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_r$ carries degree $2r$. [F3, F6, step 1.3]

2.3 Hilbert series: applying the Euler characteristic to the finite free resolution $K(\mathbf w;S)$ of $C$ gives $$\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})\cdot\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t)=\frac{\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})}{(1-t^2)^r}=\prod_i(1+t^2+\cdots+t^{2(d_i-1)}),$$ the last equality by cancelling one factor $1-t^2$ per invariant. Hence $\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$ is a polynomial of degree $2N$ with leading coefficient $1$, so $\dim_{\mathbb C}C_{2N}=1$ and $C_j=0$ for $j>2N$; the classical formula [F4] gives the same series after substituting $t^2$ for $t$. [F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Comparing steps 2.1 and 2.2 through the natural isomorphism [F6] identifies the top Koszul homology of step 2.2 with a one-dimensional space in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$; shifting back by the degree $2r$ of the top exterior generator, the space $\{c\in C:x_ic=0\text{ for all }i\}$ is one dimensional and concentrated in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i-2r=2\sum_i(d_i-1)=2N$. [F6, step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 Since $C_+=(x_1,\dots,x_r)C$ by step 1.1, the space of step 3.1 is exactly the socle $\operatorname{soc}(C)=\{c\in C:C_+c=0\}$; it is one dimensional in degree $2N$. The top graded piece $C_{2N}$ is one dimensional by step 2.3, and every element of $C_{2N}$ is annihilated by $C_+$ because $C$ has no degrees above $2N$; hence $0\neq C_{2N}\subseteq\operatorname{soc}(C)$ and both are one dimensional in degree $2N$, so $\operatorname{soc}(C)=C_{2N}$. [step 1.1, step 2.3, step 3.1]

5.1 Nondegeneracy of the top pairing: let $0\neq c\in C_i$ be homogeneous and consider the nonzero graded ideal $cC$ of the finite-dimensional graded algebra $C$; let $m$ be the largest degree with $(cC)_m\neq0$, so $m\le2N$ by step 2.3. Choose $0\neq y\in(cC)_m$; then $C_+y\subseteq(cC)_{>m}=0$, so $y\in\operatorname{soc}(C)=C_{2N}$ by step 4.1, forcing $m=2N$. Writing $y=cb$ with $b\in C_{2N-i}$ gives a nonzero product $cb$, so the pairing $C_i\times C_{2N-i}\to C_{2N}\cong\mathbb C$ has no nonzero left radical; by commutativity it has no nonzero right radical either, and finite-dimensionality of the two sides makes it a perfect pairing for every $i$. Hence $C$ is a graded Gorenstein algebra with one-dimensional socle in top degree $2N$. [step 2.3, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: The harmonic complement of the coinvariant algebra
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published invariant-theory
items. Let $W$ act on the Cartan space $\mathfrak h$ by reflections and on
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$ by graded algebra automorphisms, with coinvariant algebra
$C=S/I$ as in [[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]]. Then there
is a $W$-stable graded subspace $\mathcal H\subseteq S$, finite dimensional of
dimension $|W|$, such that the multiplication map
$$S^W\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H\longrightarrow S,\qquad p\otimes h\mapsto ph,$$
is an isomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules, and the
restriction of the quotient map $\rho:S\to C$ to $\mathcal H$ is an isomorphism
of graded $W$-modules $\mathcal H\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }C$. One may take
$$\mathcal H=\{f\in S:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\},$$
using constant-coefficient differential operators from a $W$-invariant
positive definite form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$. Any $W$-stable graded
complement of $I$ has the same multiplication and quotient properties. This
is the simultaneous kernel of all positive-degree invariant differential
operators, not in general the kernel of the quadratic Laplacian alone. In particular $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$ and
$\sum_d\dim\mathcal H_d=|W|$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose an arbitrary positive definite symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ and average it over the finite group $W$, obtaining a $W$-invariant positive definite form $(\ ,\ )$; choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ for it. On the symmetric algebra $S=\mathbb C[e_1,\dots,e_r]$ let $\langle\ ,\ \rangle$ be the Fischer pairing, the sesquilinear form with $\langle e^{\alpha},e^{\beta}\rangle=\alpha!\,\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ on monomials $e^{\alpha}$ ($\alpha$ a multi-index); it is positive definite, and $W$ acts on $S$ by orthogonal transformations for it because the form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ is $W$-invariant. For $p\in S$ let $\partial_p=p(\partial_1,\dots,\partial_r)$ be substitution of the partial derivatives $\partial_i=\partial/\partial e_i$; then multiplication by $p$ has adjoint $\partial_{\overline p}$, i.e. $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_{\overline p}g\rangle$, as checked on monomials. Choose real basic invariants: real and imaginary parts of complex invariants are invariant, and one may choose a real homogeneous basis of the indecomposables of the invariant algebra and lift it; its complexification gives basic generators. Complex conjugation preserves $S^W_+$, so simultaneous kernels are unchanged. Set $\mathcal H_d:=I_d^{\perp}$ inside the finite-dimensional space $S_d$, and $\mathcal H:=\bigoplus_d\mathcal H_d$. [F3, construct]

1.2 The invariant ring acts on $S$ with the expected Hilbert series: $S$ has a finite homogeneous $S^W$-basis by [F1], say of degrees $m_1,\dots,m_{|W|}$; their images in $S/S^W_+S=C$ form a $\mathbb C$-basis by graded Nakayama, so $\sum_jt^{m_j}=\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$ and therefore $\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By step 1.1 the spaces $S_d=I_d\oplus\mathcal H_d$ are orthogonal direct sums and $\mathcal H$ is a graded subspace; it is $W$-stable because $W$ preserves the form and $I$ is a $W$-stable homogeneous ideal, and $\mathcal H$ is a graded complement of $I$. Moreover $\mathcal H_d=\{f\in S_d:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\}$: since $I=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$, one has $f\in I_d^{\perp}$ exactly when $\langle f,w_ig\rangle=0$ for every $i$ and every $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$, which by adjointness is $\langle\partial_{w_i}f,g\rangle=0$ for all such $g$, hence $\partial_{w_i}f=0$ by positive definiteness; and for $p=\sum_iq_iw_i$ one has $\partial_p=\sum_i\partial_{q_i}\partial_{w_i}$, so vanishing for the $w_i$ is vanishing for all of $S^W_+$. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The restriction $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\to C$ is an isomorphism of graded vector spaces because $\rho$ has kernel $I$ and $\mathcal H$ is a complement of $I$ by step 1.1; it is a map of $W$-modules because $\rho$ is $W$-equivariant. Hence $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$, and $\dim\mathcal H=\dim C=|W|$ by [F2]. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $\varphi:S^W\otimes\mathcal H\to S$, $p\otimes h\mapsto ph$. This is a homomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules. Its reduction modulo $S^W_+$, namely $\mathcal H\to C$, $h\mapsto\rho(h)$, is surjective because it is the isomorphism $\rho|_{\mathcal H}$ of step 2.2. [step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 The map $\varphi$ is surjective: given homogeneous $f\in S_d$, choose $h\in\mathcal H_d$ with $\rho(f)=\rho(h)$ by step 3.1; then $f-h\in I_d=\sum_i(w_iS)_d=\sum_iw_iS_{d-2d_i}$, so by induction on $d$ each $w_ig$ with $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$ lies in $S^W\cdot\mathcal H$, and adding $h$ exhibits $f$ in the image. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The map $\varphi$ is injective: by steps 1.2 and 2.2 the two sides have the same Hilbert series, $$\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W\otimes\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t),$$ both are graded with finite-dimensional graded pieces, and by step 4.1 the kernel of the surjective graded $S^W$-linear map $\varphi$ would otherwise contribute positive Hilbert series. Hence $\varphi$ is an isomorphism. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Steps 2.1, 2.2 and 5.1 give a $W$-stable graded complement $\mathcal H$ of $I$ with $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\cong C$ and $S^W\otimes\mathcal H\cong S$; the description of $\mathcal H$ as the simultaneous invariant differential kernel follows from the adjointness $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_{\overline p}g\rangle$ of step 1.1, and $\dim\mathcal H=|W|$ by step 2.2. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory suppliers [F1] and [F2]; the construction itself uses only finite averages and finite-dimensional linear algebra. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 5.1] ∎

items.title: The deformed category O family over the Cartan symmetric algebra
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block theory
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $S=S(\mathfrak h)$ be the symmetric algebra of
the Cartan subalgebra of [[def-bgg-category-o]], graded by $\deg\mathfrak h=2$
as fixed on this page ([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]],
[[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]]). Let
$\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$ act on $S\otimes\mathbb C_\lambda$
by
$$x\cdot(s\otimes1)=xs\otimes1+\lambda(x)s\otimes1\quad(x\in\mathfrak h),\qquad x\cdot(s\otimes1)=0\quad(x\in\mathfrak n^+),$$
where for $x\in\mathfrak h$, $xs$ means multiplication by the
linear polynomial $x\in S(\mathfrak h)$; $\mathfrak n^+$ acts trivially. Put
$$M_S(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}(S\otimes\mathbb C_\lambda),$$
a module over $\mathfrak g\otimes S$: the left $\mathfrak g$-action is induced,
and $S$ acts on the right by multiplication on the last factor, which commutes
with $\mathfrak g$. Specializing at a closed point $\epsilon$ of
$\operatorname{Spec} S$ gives
$$M_S(\lambda)\otimes_S\mathbb C_\epsilon\cong M(\lambda+\epsilon),$$
the Verma module of [[def-verma-module]]; this is the universal family of
Verma modules with deformation parameter $\epsilon$.

**The family.** For a localization $T$ of $S$ put
$M_T(\lambda):=M_S(\lambda)\otimes_S T$, and let $\mathcal D_T(\lambda)$ be the
full subcategory of $\mathfrak g\otimes T$-modules that are direct summands of
a finite direct sum of modules $E\otimes M_T(\lambda)$ for finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak g$-modules $E$. Write $\mathcal D_R(\lambda)$ for
$R=S_{(0)}$, the localization of $S$ at the origin of
$\operatorname{Spec} S$. The **deformed family** is the assignment
$T\mapsto\mathcal D_T(\lambda)$ together with the specialization functors
$-\otimes_T\mathbb C_\epsilon$ at the closed points $\epsilon$ of
$\operatorname{Spec} T$. By the tensor identity for finite-dimensional modules
and the Verma flags of tensor products
([[lem-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-verma-flags]]) the
specializations have Verma constituents of highest weights
$\lambda+\nu+\epsilon$, where $\nu$ runs through the weights of the
finite-dimensional tensor factors, and they can meet several
central-character blocks, whose labels are the dot-Weyl orbits through these
highest weights ([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]); a generic
parameter is generally nonintegral, and the distinct constituent labels have distinct central characters at the
generic parameter: an equality $\lambda+\gamma+\tau+\rho=w(\lambda+\gamma'+\tau+\rho)$
as affine functions of $\tau$ forces $w=1$ by comparing linear parts,
and then $\gamma=\gamma'$ ([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]).

**Selected components.** For a regular dominant integral source $\lambda$ as in
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]] and a
dot-dominant integral target $\nu$, so that $\nu+\rho$ lies in the closed
positive chamber, denote by $\mathcal D_R^{[\nu]}(\lambda)$ the component of
$\mathcal D_R(\lambda)$ whose closed fiber at the origin lies in the selected
target block $\mathcal O_\nu$ of
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]]. Finite Verma flags of the
deformed tensor products and pairwise-unit resultants of their
central-character polynomials define this component by actual central
idempotents over $R$, obtained from [[thm-chinese-remainder-theorem-for-comaximal-ideals]].
Indeed choose a linear combination $z$ of central elements separating the
finitely many distinct special characters. On each deformed Verma factor,
$z$ acts by a polynomial $c_i(\tau)$ by
[[lem-harish-chandra-projection-computes-highest-weight-scalars]], and a flag
is annihilated by $\prod_i(z-c_i(\tau))$. Group these factors by their
constant values at the origin; differences from different groups are units
in $R$, so their product polynomials are comaximal in $R[X]$. CRT gives
mutually orthogonal polynomial projectors, whose images are the selected
components and whose sum is the identity. Other central-character components remain part of the full tensor
family; thus whole-family statements and selected-block statements are
distinguished.

**Weight structure.** Write $\tau:\mathfrak h\to T$ for the tautological linear map.
Modules in $\mathcal D_T(\lambda)$ carry a **deformed weight decomposition**
$X=\bigoplus_\xi X^\xi$, where
$$X^\xi=\{m:(h-\tau(h))m=\xi(h)m\text{ for every }h\in\mathfrak h\}.$$
These are eigenmodules for $h-\tau(h)$, not ordinary complex weight spaces
for $h$. They are finite projective, hence locally free of finite rank over $T$, as follows from the PBW model of Verma modules and the
flatness of the localization
([[thm-pbw-ordered-monomial-basis-for-the-enveloping-algebra]]). The
conventions are those of [Soe90, Section 2.1]; no choice beyond the inherited
Axiom of Choice of the block theory is used.
items.strategy: The construction is the standard universal family of Verma modules with a formal deformation parameter; the twisted $\mathfrak b$-action makes the fiber at $\epsilon$ the Verma module of weight $\lambda+\epsilon$, the right $S$-action commutes with $\mathfrak g$, and direct summands of finite tensor products give the analogue of the projective functors of [[def-projective-functors-on-a-regular-integral-category-o-block]] over $T$. Weight spaces are locally free by the PBW model of Verma modules; no choice beyond the inherited AC of the block theory is used. Tensor products have finite Verma flags by the PBW tensor identity and the weight filtration of the finite-dimensional b-module E; the deformed flag factors are M_T(lambda+nu). Direct-summand flags over local R follow by canonical maximal-weight peeling: U(g)X^nu=Delta_R(nu) tensor_R X^nu for a maximal label, every idempotent preserves this submodule, its top-weight image is finite free, and induction applies to the quotient. For selected components choose a central element separating the finitely many special central characters of these factors; its grouped annihilating polynomials have pairwise-unit resultants and hence Chinese-remainder projectors in R[X], which become actual central projectors. Thus whole-family statements and selected-block statements are distinguished. The generic regular/nonintegral Verma assertion follows from the Shapovalov determinant factors; generic here means the generic point or parameters avoiding the countably many reducibility hyperplanes, not a Zariski-open set on which integrality persists.

items.title: The nilpotent central fiber is reduced and integral
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and Weyl group $W$,
and let $p_1,\dots,p_r$ be homogeneous basic generators of $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}$
of degrees $d_1,\dots,d_r$, corresponding by Chevalley restriction to basic Weyl
invariants ([[thm-symmetric-invariants-restrict-to-weyl-invariants]],
[[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]]). Put
$$A=S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r).$$ Then $A$ is a reduced integral domain of
dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r=2|\Phi^+|$, with Hilbert series
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(A,t)=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{d_i})}{(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}},$$
and for every central character $\chi:Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\mathbb C$ the PBW
associated graded of $U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$ is canonically
isomorphic to $A$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $\mathfrak g=0$ then $r=0$ and $A=\mathbb C$, so all assertions hold; assume otherwise. By [F1], $S(\mathfrak g)$ is free over the polynomial invariant algebra $\mathbb C[p_1,\ldots,p_r]$. After quotienting by the first $j$ generators it remains free over $\mathbb C[p_{j+1},\ldots,p_r]$; hence multiplication by the next generator is injective and all successive quotients are nonzero. Thus the $p_i$ form a regular sequence, rather than merely a sequence of algebraically independent elements. The Koszul Euler characteristic gives $\operatorname{Hilb}(A,t)=\prod_i(1-t^{d_i})/(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}$. At any rational maximal ideal containing the $p_i$, the ambient polynomial local ring has dimension $\dim\mathfrak g$: the chain of translated coordinate ideals gives this lower bound at a rational point, and [[cor-dimension-of-a-finite-polynomial-ring-over-a-field]] gives the upper bound, and [F2] gives quotient dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r$. At every prime the same regular sequence localizes and [F2] makes the quotient Cohen--Macaulay. In particular $\dim A=\dim\mathfrak g-r=2N$ by root-space decomposition. The Hilbert series has pole order $2N$ at $t=1$; it is not a polynomial of degree $2N$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Choose for every simple root $\alpha_i$ an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $(e_i,f_i,h_i)$ and write $2\rho^\vee=\sum_i c_i h_i$ in the simple-coroot basis, so $\sum_i c_i\alpha_j(h_i)=2$ for every simple root $\alpha_j$, and put $e=\sum_i e_i$, $h=2\rho^\vee$, $f=\sum_i c_i f_i$. Distinct simple-root differences are not roots, so $[e_i,f_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$, and consequently $[h,e]=2e$, $[h,f]=-2f$ and $[e,f]=h$. The eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}h$ are $2\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$ and zero, hence all are even. Complete reducibility for this $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ subalgebra writes the adjoint module as a direct sum of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-strings $L(2m_1)\oplus\cdots$; each string contributes exactly one vector killed by $h$, and $\ker\operatorname{ad}h=\mathfrak h$ has dimension $r$, so there are exactly $r$ strings; a string with $m_j=0$ would consist of a nonzero vector killed by $e$ and $h$, i.e. a nonzero element of $\mathfrak h$ commuting with all $e_i$, which is central in $\mathfrak g$, hence zero; so all $m_j\ge1$ and counting dimensions gives $\sum_j(2m_j+1)=\dim\mathfrak g=2N+r$, that is $\sum_jm_j=N$. The highest vector of a string has $\operatorname{ad}h$-eigenvalue $2m_j>0$, hence lies in $\mathfrak n^+=\bigoplus_{\alpha>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$; therefore $\ker\operatorname{ad}e$ is the $r$-dimensional span of the highest vectors and lies in $\mathfrak n^+$, and the lowest vectors span $z_f:=\ker\operatorname{ad}f\subseteq\mathfrak n^-$ with $\mathfrak g=[\mathfrak g,e]\oplus z_f$. [F3, algebra]

1.3 Let $\varphi_t(x)=t\cdot\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-\rho^\vee})(x)$ for $t\in\mathbb C^\times$. Since $p_i$ is $\mathfrak g$-invariant, $p_i(\varphi_tx)=t^{d_i}p_i(x)$ for all $x\in\mathfrak g$; since $\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-\rho^\vee})f_i=tf_i$, the map $\varphi_t$ preserves $z_f$, so with $q_i(y):=p_i(e+y)$ one has $q_i(\varphi_ty)=p_i(\varphi_t(e+y))=t^{d_i}q_i(y)$: each $q_i$ is weighted-homogeneous of weighted degree $d_i$ for the weights $\deg y_j=m_j+1$ on $z_f$; indeed a root vector of height $t$ has $\varphi$-weight $1-t$, so the lowest vector $y_j$ has weight $m_j+1\ge2$. [F3, algebra]

2.1 The group constructions needed below are explicit. Order the height spaces of $\mathfrak g$ by root height, with $\mathfrak h$ at height zero. The endomorphisms $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+$ strictly raise height. Exponential and logarithm are finite inverse polynomials on the corresponding strictly triangular matrices. For a unipotent automorphism $u$ which raises height relative to the identity, $\exp(t\log u)$ preserves the Lie bracket for every integer $t$ since it equals $u^t$; the bracket equations are polynomial in $t$, so they hold for all complex $t$. Differentiating at zero shows that $\log u$ is a derivation. By [F4] it equals $\operatorname{ad}x$; comparison of the height components shows $x\in\mathfrak n^+$, because negative-root components lower height and a Cartan component acts in height zero, and $\operatorname{ad}$ is injective. Thus $N_+=\exp(\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+)$ is exactly the closed subgroup of $G$ defined by these strict-height unipotence equations; it is polynomially isomorphic to $\mathfrak n^+$, hence connected. Let $H=(\mathbb C^\times)^r$ act by fixing $\mathfrak h$ and multiplying $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ by $\prod_i t_i^{a_i}$ when $\alpha=\sum_i a_i\alpha_i$. Root brackets show this is a closed torus of automorphisms, with Lie algebra $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak h$. It normalizes $N_+$; $B=HN_+$ is closed, since the diagonal entries determine its $H$ factor and the remaining strict-height unipotent equations determine its $N_+$ factor. It is connected and solvable, with Lie algebra $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak b$. Any Lie subalgebra containing $\mathfrak b$ is $\mathfrak h$-stable and splits into root spaces; if it is larger it contains a negative root space and hence, together with its positive root space, a root $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, so it cannot be solvable. Thus $B$ is maximal among connected solvable closed subgroups (a larger such subgroup would have larger solvable Lie algebra), and is a Borel. The connected group $G=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)^0$ is smooth and irreducible of dimension $\dim\mathfrak g$ by [F4], and its Borels are conjugate. These explicit tori also give the height scalings used in step 1.3. [F3, F4, algebra]

2.2 The central reduction has associated graded $A$: fix a central character $\chi:Z\to\mathbb C$ with kernel $\mathfrak m_\chi$, and let $J=\mathfrak m_\chi U(\mathfrak g)$. By [F6], $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)=S(\mathfrak g)$, $\operatorname{gr}Z=S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}$, and the leading symbol of any $z\in\mathfrak m_\chi$ lies in $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}_+=(p_1,\dots,p_r)$; conversely each $p_i$ is the leading symbol of an element of $\mathfrak m_\chi$, for instance of $z_i-\chi(z_i)$ for a central element $z_i$ of leading symbol $p_i$ (the scalar term has lower filtration degree because $d_i>0$). Therefore $\operatorname{gr}J=(p_1,\dots,p_r)S(\mathfrak g)$ and the natural graded surjection $S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{gr}(U(\mathfrak g)/J)$ is an isomorphism: both sides have the Hilbert series of step 1.1, since the filtered free harmonic decomposition of [F6] restricts to a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)/J$ whose symbols have exactly the Hilbert series $\prod_i(1-t^{d_i})/(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}$. Hence the PBW associated graded of $U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$ is canonically $A$. [F6, step 1.1]

3.1 The morphism $\Psi:G\times z_f\to\mathfrak g$, $(g,y)\mapsto g\cdot(e+y)$, is dominant. Its differential at $(1,0)$ is $(\xi,y)\mapsto[\xi,e]+y$ for $\xi\in T_1G=\mathfrak g$ (using $G$-equivariance of the action), with image $[\mathfrak g,e]+z_f=\mathfrak g$ by step 1.2; hence the cotangent map is injective and, by the submersion criterion at the rational points $(1,0)$ and $e$, $\Psi$ is locally standard smooth, hence flat, at $(1,0)$; the flat locus is open and flat morphisms of finite presentation are open, so the image of $\Psi$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathfrak g$; since $\mathfrak g$ is irreducible, $\Psi$ is dominant. [F5, step 1.2, step 2.1]

3.2 If $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent, $U_x=\{\exp(t\operatorname{ad}x):t\in\mathbb C\}$ is a closed connected unipotent subgroup of $G$: for $x\ne0$ logarithm identifies it with the closed line $\mathbb C\operatorname{ad}x$; for $x=0$ it is trivial. Among connected solvable closed subgroups containing it choose one of maximal dimension; any strictly larger connected closed subgroup has larger dimension, so it is a Borel. Conjugacy from [F4] moves it into the $B$ constructed in step 2.1. Every unipotent element of that triangular group has diagonal entries all one, hence trivial $H$ factor, and lies in $N_+$. Its logarithm therefore belongs to $\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+$ by step 2.1. Injectivity and equivariance of $\operatorname{ad}$ show that $x$ is conjugate into $\mathfrak n^+$. Conversely the invariant $p_i$ vanishes on $\mathfrak n^+$: the torus automorphism multiplying height $j$ by $t^j$ sends every $n\in\mathfrak n^+$ to zero as $t\to0$, while invariance preserves $p_i(n)$. Thus $p_i(n)=p_i(0)=0$. Lie invariance implies $G$-invariance here: the differential of $g\mapsto p_i(gx)$ vanishes on the connected smooth group, and in characteristic zero a regular function with zero differential on an irreducible variety is constant. [F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The restrictions $q_1,\dots,q_r\in\mathbb C[z_f]$ are algebraically independent: the pullback $\Psi^*$ is injective because $\Psi$ is dominant, and $\Psi^*(p_i)=q_i$ by $G$-invariance of the $p_i$; if a nonzero polynomial $F$ satisfied $F(q_1,\dots,q_r)=0$, then $\Psi^*(F(p_1,\dots,p_r))=0$, hence $F(p_1,\dots,p_r)=0$ in $S(\mathfrak g)$, contradicting the algebraic independence of $p_1,\dots,p_r$ from [F1]. [F1, step 3.1]

4.2 The common zero set $\mathcal N=\{x:p_i(x)=0\text{ for all }i\}$ equals $G\cdot\mathfrak n^+$: the inclusion $\supseteq$ is step 3.2, and conversely if all $p_i$ vanish then every invariant polynomial of positive degree vanishes, so the invariant traces $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{ad}x)^k)$, $k\ge1$, vanish because each is invariant with zero constant term; Newton's identities express every coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of $\operatorname{ad}x$ polynomially in these traces, so the characteristic polynomial is $T^{\dim\mathfrak g}$, hence $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent and $x$ is conjugate into $\mathfrak n^+$ by step 3.2. Also $\mathcal N$ is the underlying set of $\operatorname{Spec}A$. [F3, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 The map $q=(q_1,\dots,q_r):\mathbb A^r\to\mathbb A^r$ is dominant by step 4.1, and $\mathbb A^r$ is smooth, so generic smoothness provides a dense open subset of $\mathbb A^r$ on which the differential of $q$ is surjective; in particular the Jacobian determinant $D=\det(\partial q_i/\partial y_j)$ is not identically zero. [F5, step 4.1]

6.1 Weights: $D$ is weighted-homogeneous of weighted degree $\sum_id_i-\sum_j(m_j+1)=\sum_i(d_i-1)-\sum_jm_j=N-N=0$ by steps 1.2 and 1.3, because the derivative with respect to $y_j$ lowers weighted degree by $m_j+1$; a nonzero polynomial all of whose monomials have positive weights $m_j+1$ and total weighted degree zero is a nonzero constant. Hence $D$ is a nonzero constant, and in particular the linear map $z_f\to\mathbb C^r$, $y\mapsto(dp_1(e)(y),\dots,dp_r(e)(y))$, given by the matrix $(\partial q_i/\partial y_j)(0)$, is invertible. [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 The Jacobian matrix of the presentation $A=S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r)$ at the rational maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $e$ has rank exactly $r$: its rows are the differentials $dp_i(e)$, which are linearly independent by step 6.1. Since $\dim A_{\mathfrak m}=\dim A=\dim\mathfrak g-r$ by step 1.1, the Jacobian criterion in the form $\operatorname{rank}J(\mathfrak m)=n-\dim A_{\mathfrak m}$ identifies $A_{\mathfrak m}$ as a regular local ring. [F5, step 1.1, step 6.1]

8.1 The set $\mathcal N$ is irreducible: step 4.2 identifies its closed points with the image of the irreducible variety $G\times\mathfrak n^+$, so its closure is irreducible and equals the underlying space of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ ([[cor-closed-points-dense-in-affine-spectra]] and [[cor-weak-nullstellensatz-algebraically-closed-coordinate-form]] give density of its complex rational closed points). In particular there is a unique minimal prime $\mathfrak p_0$. The regular local ring $A_{\mathfrak m_e}$ of step 7.1 localizes further to $A_{\mathfrak p_0}$; localizations of regular local rings are regular by [[cor-localisations-of-regular-local-rings-are-regular]]. Since $\mathfrak p_0$ is minimal, that localization has dimension zero and is a field. This proves generic reducedness without needing an assertion about openness of the regular orbit. [F5, step 4.2, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 There are no embedded associated primes. For $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(A)$ choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\supseteq\mathfrak q$. An element with annihilator $\mathfrak q$ remains nonzero at $\mathfrak m$ and has annihilator $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak m}$, so this is an associated prime of $A_{\mathfrak m}$. That local ring is Cohen--Macaulay by step 1.1, and the associated-prime theorem in [F2] makes $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak m}$ minimal. Any strict smaller prime of $A$ below $\mathfrak q$ would remain strict after localization at $\mathfrak m$, so $\mathfrak q$ itself is minimal. Hence the only possible associated prime is the unique $\mathfrak p_0$ of step 8.1. The associated-localization detection map in [F5] therefore injects $A$ into the field $A_{\mathfrak p_0}$, proving that $A$ is an integral domain and in particular reduced. The Cohen--Macaulay argument is essential here; generic reducedness alone would not exclude embedded nilpotents. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 8.1, algebra]

10.1 Combining steps 1.1, 2.2, 9.1: $A$ is a reduced integral domain of dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r=2N=2|\Phi^+|$ with the displayed Hilbert series, and every central reduction has associated graded $A$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory, group-theoretic and geometric suppliers [F1], [F4], [F5] and [F6]; the conclusions themselves are choice-free statements about $\mathfrak g$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 9.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: The wall-crossing functor and its unit and counit
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block and
translation theory ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]]).

Fix the dominant regular integral representative $\lambda$ of a regular
integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$
([[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]]) and an
integral weight $\mu$ such that $\lambda+\rho$ is regular dominant and
$\mu+\rho$ is dominant with dot stabilizer exactly $\{1,s\}$ for a reflection
$s=s_\alpha$; this is the dominant-chamber version of single-wall translation
data, the published
[[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]] being stated with
antidominant representatives, and the dominant standard counts below are
proved through the norm-distance and extremal-weight bounds
([[lem-dominant-norm-distance-comparison]],
[[lem-weight-norm-bound-for-finite-dimensional-simple-modules]]) rather than
by applying that datum literally. Let $\nu$ be the unique dominant element of
the linear Weyl orbit of $\mu-\lambda$ and let
$E=L(\nu)$ be the finite-dimensional simple module of highest weight $\nu$, so
that $\mu-\lambda$ is an extremal weight of $E$; write
$E^{*}=L(-w_0\nu)$ for its dual
([[prop-highest-weight-of-the-dual-representation]]).

With $\chi_\lambda,\chi_\mu$ the generalized central characters and
$\operatorname{pr}$ the exact central projections of
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], define the **onto-wall** and
**out-of-wall** translations
$$T_{\mathrm{on}}:=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}\circ(E\otimes-)\big|_{\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda}},\qquad T_{\mathrm{out}}:=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}\circ(E^{*}\otimes-)\big|_{\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu}},$$
and the **wall-crossing functor**
$$\theta_s:=T_{\mathrm{out}}\circ T_{\mathrm{on}}\colon\mathcal O_\lambda\longrightarrow\mathcal O_\lambda .$$

**Basic properties.** Both translations are exact, and $T_{\mathrm{out}}$ is
both a left and a right adjoint of $T_{\mathrm{on}}$
([[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]]); hence
$\theta_s$ is exact and, as a composite of restriction-of-scalars and central
block projection applied to tensoring by $E^{*}\otimes E$, it is a natural
direct summand of the endofunctor
$\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}\circ((E^{*}\otimes E)\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_{\chi_\lambda}$,
so it is a projective functor on $\mathcal O_\lambda$ in the sense of
[[def-projective-functors-on-a-regular-integral-category-o-block]]. On
standard objects the dominant-chamber counts are
$T_{\mathrm{on}}\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ and the
two-factor flag $[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(w\cdot s\cdot\lambda)]$ for
$T_{\mathrm{out}}\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$, as follows directly from the tensor flag and the two norm bounds above.
Put $v=\lambda+\rho$, $u=\mu+\rho$. A retained onto-wall label satisfies
$wv+\gamma=xu$ with $|\gamma|\le|u-v|$. Thus
$|\gamma|=|v-w^{-1}xu|\ge|v-u|$; equality and regularity of $v$ give
$w^{-1}xu=u$, leaving the single label $w\cdot\mu$, with its extremal
weight of multiplicity one. For the return translation,
$wu+\delta=xv$ implies equality in $|u-w^{-1}xv|\ge|u-v|$, so
$w^{-1}xv\in\{v,sv\}$ and $x\in\{w,ws\}$, again with
extremal weights of multiplicity one. These calculations use the Verma
tensor flag of [[lem-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-verma-flags]].

**Unit and counit.** The two tensor-block adjunctions supply natural
transformations
$$\eta\colon\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal O_\lambda}\longrightarrow\theta_s,\qquad\varepsilon\colon\theta_s\longrightarrow\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal O_\lambda},$$
where $\eta$ is the unit of the adjunction $T_{\mathrm{on}}\dashv T_{\mathrm{out}}$
and $\varepsilon$ the counit of the adjunction $T_{\mathrm{out}}\dashv T_{\mathrm{on}}$;
each satisfies the triangle identities with its companion counit or unit on
the wall category, and these identities are part of the data. The pair
$(\theta_s,\eta,\varepsilon)$ is determined by the choice of the
biadjunction maps, which are fixed once and for all.

**Independence of the auxiliary weight.** Up to natural equivalence the
functor $\theta_s$ depends only on the wall $s$ and the block
$\mathcal O_\lambda$, not on the chosen ambient weight $\mu$: this
well-definedness statement is discharged forward by
[[thm-indecomposable-projective-functors-are-indexed-by-the-weyl-group]],
which lifts the equality of the evaluations on standard objects to a natural
equivalence; it is recorded in `justified_by` and is not used to construct
$\theta_s$ or to generate objects.
items.strategy: Exactness and biadjunction follow from finite-dimensional tensor-Hom pairing and exact central block inclusion/projection. The singular block projection is a natural idempotent on E tensor -, so composing it with E* tensor - gives the asserted summand of a single tensor functor. The dominant-chamber standard counts are proved by the general dominant norm-distance and extremal-weight bound, not by applying the printed antidominant-only datum literally. Their two-factor class on the dominant Verma is Delta_e+Delta_s. BGG reciprocity and the one-dimensional simple-root lowered weight give P_s the same flag; hence theta_s Delta_e=P_s. The later proved projective-functor classification lifts equality of these evaluations to natural equivalence, proving wall-weight independence. This is a forward well-definedness discharge, declared in justified_by, not a circular prerequisite for chosen-wall construction or object generation.

items.title: The coinvariant algebra is the graded regular representation of W
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published invariant-theory
items. Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group with reflection representation
$\mathfrak h$, coinvariant algebra $C=S(\mathfrak h)/S(\mathfrak h)S^W_+$ and
classical basic degrees $d_1,\dots,d_r$ as in
[[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]] and
[[lem-the-coinvariant-algebra-is-a-gorenstein-algebra-with-one-dimensional-socle]].
Then:

1. $C\cong\mathbb C W$ as a $W$-module: the coinvariant algebra is isomorphic
to the regular representation of $W$.
2. The graded $W$-character of $C$ is
$$\operatorname{HTr}(C,t)(w)=\sum_{i\ge0}t^i\operatorname{tr}(w\mid C_i)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{2d_i})\cdot\det(1-t^2w\mid\mathfrak h^*)^{-1}\qquad(w\in W),$$
an identity of rational functions whose limit at $t=1$ is $|W|$ for $w=1$ and
$0$ for $w\neq1$.
3. Equivalently, $C$ is the graded lift of the regular representation: if
$\operatorname{mult}_E(C,t)$ denotes the graded multiplicity of the irreducible
$W$-module $E$, then the identity
$\sum_E\operatorname{mult}_E(C,t)\chi_E(w)=\operatorname{HTr}(C,t)(w)$
determines the graded multiplicities uniquely, with
$\operatorname{mult}_E(C,1)=\dim E$. The Hilbert-series specialization of (2)
at $w=1$ is $\prod_i(1+t^2+\cdots+t^{2(d_i-1)})$, the published coinvariant
Hilbert series in the page normalization $\deg\mathfrak h=2$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\xrightarrow{\sim}C$ is an isomorphism of graded $W$-modules, so the graded traces agree: $\operatorname{HTr}(C,t)(w)=\operatorname{HTr}(\mathcal H,t)(w)$ for every $w\in W$. [F1]

1.2 Molien's formula for the graded trace of $S$: for $|t|<1$ and $w\in W$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r$ on $\mathfrak h^*$, one has $\operatorname{tr}(w\mid S_i)=h_i(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r)$, the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial of degree $i$, whose generating function is $\sum_{i\ge0}h_i(\lambda)t^i=\prod_j(1-t\lambda_j)^{-1}$; with page degrees doubled this gives $\operatorname{HTr}(S,t)(w)=\det(1-t^2w\mid\mathfrak h^*)^{-1}$ as an identity of formal power series, the finite sum over the eigenvalues making every coefficient finite. [algebra]

1.3 Since $S\cong S^W\otimes\mathcal H$ with $W$ acting trivially on the polynomial ring $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$, whose homogeneous piece of page degree $2D$ has dimension equal to the number of monomials of weighted degree $D$, the graded trace factors as $\operatorname{HTr}(S,t)(w)=\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})^{-1}\cdot\operatorname{HTr}(\mathcal H,t)(w)$ for $|t|<1$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Combining steps 1.1 to 1.3, $$\operatorname{HTr}(C,t)(w)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{2d_i})\cdot\operatorname{HTr}(S,t)(w)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{2d_i})\cdot\det(1-t^2w\mid\mathfrak h^*)^{-1},$$ first as an identity of formal power series for $|t|<1$ and then as an identity of rational functions; this is assertion (2). [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3]

3.1 Limits at $t\to1$: each factor $1-t^{2d_i}$ vanishes to order exactly one at $t=1$ because its derivative there is $-2d_i\neq0$, so the numerator vanishes to order $r$. The denominator $\det(1-t^2w\mid\mathfrak h^*)=\prod_j(1-t^2\lambda_j)$ vanishes at $t=1$ to the order of the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $1$ of $w$ on $\mathfrak h^*$, that is, to order $\dim\mathfrak h^w$; the reflection representation is faithful, so $w\neq1$ implies $\mathfrak h^w\neq\mathfrak h$ and $\dim\mathfrak h^w\le r-1$, whence for $w\neq1$ the limit of $\operatorname{HTr}(C,t)(w)$ is $0$. At $w=1$ the quotient is $\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})/(1-t^2)^r\to\prod_id_i=|W|$ by [F2]. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The graded trace at $t=1$ is the ordinary character of the finite-dimensional $W$-module $C$, so step 3.1 shows $\chi_C(w)=|W|\delta_{w,1}$, the character of the regular representation; by the orthonormality of irreducible characters [F3], the multiplicity of each irreducible $E$ in $C$ equals its multiplicity in $\mathbb C W$, namely $\dim E$. Hence $C\cong\mathbb C W$ as $W$-modules, which is assertion (1). [F3, step 3.1]

5.1 Graded multiplicities: each homogeneous piece of $C$ decomposes into isotypic components, giving each irreducible $E$ its uniquely determined graded multiplicity series $\operatorname{mult}_E(C,t)$, and the identities $\sum_E\operatorname{mult}_E(C,t)\chi_E(w)=\operatorname{HTr}(C,t)(w)$ for all $w$ determine $\operatorname{mult}_E(C,t)$ as the coefficient of $\chi_E$ in the expansion of the graded character in the orthonormal basis of [F3]; setting $t=1$ recovers $\operatorname{mult}_E(C,1)$ as the multiplicity of $E$ in $C$, which is $\dim E$ by step 4.1; this is assertion (3). The Hilbert-series specialization of step 2.1 at $w=1$ is $\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})/(1-t^2)^r=\prod_i(1+t^2+\cdots+t^{2(d_i-1)})$. [F3, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎
