items.title: The antidominant projective and the Soergel functor
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block theory
([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]]).

In the regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$ of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]] fix the
antidominant weight $w_0\cdot\lambda$ and let
$$P:=P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$$ be a projective cover of $L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]); it is unique up to isomorphism and
indecomposable ([[prop-projective-covers-in-o-are-indecomposable-and-unique]],
[[def-projective-object]]), and it is an injective object of
$\mathcal O_\lambda$. The **Soergel functor** is
$$V:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,-)\colon\mathcal O_\lambda\longrightarrow \operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}\text{-}\mathbf{mod},\qquad M\longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,M),$$
with the left action of $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}$ on
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,M)$ induced by composition on the right of
the source: $a\cdot f=f\circ a$
([[def-projective-functors-on-a-regular-integral-category-o-block]]). Its
values on the standard objects and on the indecomposable projectives are
written $V\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):=V(\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))$ and
$VP(w\cdot\lambda):=V(P(w\cdot\lambda))$. The functor $V$ is exact, because
$P$ is projective, and hence left exact; the identity
$VP\cong\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)$ with its regular module structure
is the Yoneda identification. Replacing the chosen projective cover $P$ by an
isomorphic one changes $V$ by a natural equivalence of functors compatible
with the endomorphism-ring identification, so the construction depends only
on the isomorphism class of $P$.

**Well-definedness: $P$ is injective.** We prove that $P$ is an injective
object of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ using only the listed suppliers, following the
argument of [Soe90, Sections 1.2 and 2.1] in its algebraic form. Put
$\eta:=-\rho$; then $W\cdot\eta=\{\eta\}$, because $w\cdot\eta=w(\eta+\rho)-\rho=-\rho$
for every $w$ ([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]). By
[[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]] the simple
objects are the $L(\mu)$ with $L(\mu)$ determined by $\mu$, and the composition
factors of $M(\eta)$ have highest weights in $W\cdot\eta\cap(\eta-Q^+)=\{\eta\}$;
hence $M(\eta)=L(\eta)$ is simple. By BGG reciprocity
([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]) applied to the single-label block, and the existence
of Verma flags for projectives ([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]]),
the projective cover $P(\eta)$ has a Verma flag with the single factor
$\Delta(\eta)=M(\eta)=L(\eta)$, so $P(\eta)\cong L(\eta)$; the block
$\mathcal O_\eta$ has a single simple object, which is projective, hence is
semisimple by enough projectives ([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]),
and therefore every object of $\mathcal O_\eta$, in particular $L(\eta)$, is
injective as well as projective in $\mathcal O_\eta$
([[def-injective-object]]). A projective object of a block is projective in
$\mathcal O$ ([[lem-block-projection-preserves-projectives]]), and an
injective object of a block is injective in $\mathcal O$ because the block
decomposition is a direct sum of abelian subcategories and the exact
projections restrict split exactness blockwise. Second, we identify a
projective-injective object
in the block $\mathcal O_\lambda$: let $E=L(\lambda+\rho)$ be the
finite-dimensional simple module of highest weight $\lambda+\rho$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]])
and set
$$Q:=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}\bigl(E\otimes L(\eta)\bigr)\in\mathcal O_\lambda,$$
the exact central projection of [[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]].
Since $L(\eta)$ is projective and injective in $\mathcal O$, the tensor product
$E\otimes L(\eta)$ is projective and injective
([[lem-tensoring-a-projective-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-is-projective]]),
and its direct summand $Q$ is projective and injective in $\mathcal O$; the
general exact tensor-block biadjunction of
[[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]] gives the
same conclusion with all adjoints and, by
[[lem-tensoring-a-projective-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-is-projective]],
injectivity (equivalently, $Q$ is a direct summand of a projective-injective
object, and injectivity passes to summands). Third, we compute a
one-dimensional Hom space: since $M(a)$ with $a=w_0\cdot\lambda$ is simple by
the same top-weight argument as for $\eta$ (every other highest weight in
$W\cdot a$ lies strictly above $a$ in the root order), the tensor product
$E^{*}\otimes M(a)$ has a finite Verma flag whose factors are the
$\Delta(a+\nu)$ with $\nu$ running through the weights of the dual module
$E^{*}$, by
[[lem-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-verma-flags]]; here
$E^{*}=L(-w_0(\lambda+\rho))$ ([[prop-highest-weight-of-the-dual-representation]]).
Projecting to the central character $\chi_\eta$ retains exactly the factors
with $a+\nu\in W\cdot\eta=\{\eta\}$, that is $\nu=-w_0(\lambda+\rho)$, the
highest weight of $E^{*}$ of multiplicity one, so
$$\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\eta}\bigl(E^{*}\otimes M(a)\bigr)=L(\eta).$$
The tensor-hom adjunction and the tensor-block adjunction now give
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(Q,L(a))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(L(\eta),E^{*}\otimes M(a))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(L(\eta),L(\eta))\cong\mathbb C,$$
because every homomorphism from the block-$\eta$ simple lands in the
$\chi_\eta$-summand and $L(\eta)$ is simple. Choose the nonzero, hence
surjective, element $q:Q\to L(a)$ and lift it through the projective cover
$P(a)\to L(a)$ to a map $Q\to P(a)$; its image is a submodule of $P(a)$
surjecting onto the head $L(a)$, hence is all of $P(a)$ by essentiality of a
projective cover, so the lift is surjective and splits by projectivity of
$P(a)$. Therefore $P(a)$ is a direct summand of the injective object $Q$
([[def-injective-object]]), and direct summands of injective objects are
injective, so $P=P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ is injective. This argument uses
[[thm-bgg-verma-homomorphism-criterion]] only through the standard embedding
criterion implicit in the top-weight computations, and it does not assume the
Endomorphismensatz.

**The once-each flag.** The tensor flag of $E\otimes M(-\rho)$ has labels
$-\rho+\gamma$ for weights $\gamma$ of $E=L(\lambda+\rho)$. Projection to
$\chi_\lambda$ keeps precisely $\gamma\in W(\lambda+\rho)$, each of
multiplicity one by [[lem-weight-norm-bound-for-finite-dimensional-simple-modules]].
Thus $Q$ has each $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ once. Every such Verma contains
$M(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(a)$ by
[[lem-dominant-integral-dot-translates-embed-in-the-verma-module]]. BGG
reciprocity gives $(P(a):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))\ge1$; the splitting
$Q=P(a)\oplus Q'$ and
[[lem-direct-summands-of-verma-filtered-objects-are-verma-filtered]] give the
opposite bound one. Hence all these multiplicities equal one, $Q'$ has
an empty flag and is zero, and $Q=P(a)$. Since $P(a)$ is projective,
$V$ is exact and $\dim VX=[X:L(a)]$ for finite-length $X$: on simples its
values are $\mathbb C$ at the head label and zero otherwise. Consequently
$\dim V\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)=1$ for every $x$. Every simple submodule of a
Verma is itself a simple Verma: its universal Verma map into that Verma is
injective. Thus the unique simple standard $L(a)$ is its only possible
socle label, and [[thm-verma-homomorphism-spaces-have-dimension-at-most-one]]
makes this socle a single copy of $L(a)$.
items.strategy:
Injectivity has the following algebraic proof using only published suppliers. Put $\eta=-ho$. Every simple in its central-character summand has highest weight in $W\cdot\eta=\{\eta\}$, by highest-weight classification and the central-character theorem. Thus $M(\eta)=L(\eta)$: its top weight has dimension one and its finite composition series has only this simple. BGG reciprocity and a Verma flag give $P(\eta)=L(\eta)$; enough projectives then makes this one-simple block semisimple, so $L(\eta)$ is also injective. Let $E=L(\lambda+ho)$ and set $Q=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}(E\otimes L(\eta))$. The general tensor-block exact biadjunction proved in [[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]] shows that $Q$ is projective and injective. Set $a=w_0\cdot\lambda=w_0(\lambda+ho)-ho$. The same central-orbit/top-weight argument makes the antidominant $M(a)$ simple (any other highest weight in its dot orbit is strictly above $a$). Tensoring $E^*\otimes M(a)$ has a Verma flag with factors $M(a+
u)$ indexed by weights $
u$ of $E^*$. Projection to $\chi_\eta$ retains only $a+
u=-ho$, namely $
u=-w_0(\lambda+ho)$, the highest weight of $E^*$ of multiplicity one. Hence that projection is $L(\eta)$, and adjunction gives $\operatorname{Hom}(Q,L(a))=\mathbb C$. Lift the surjection $Q	o L(a)$ through the projective cover $P(a)	o L(a)$; essentiality of the cover makes the lift surjective, and projectivity of $P(a)$ splits it. Thus $P(a)$ is a summand of the injective $Q$ and is injective. This proof does not assume the Endomorphismensatz. Projectivity also makes $V$ exact (and hence left exact); independence of the chosen cover and $VP=\operatorname{End}(P)$ follow directly by composition and projective-cover uniqueness. In fact $Q=P(a)$: its projected tensor Verma flag consists of every $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ once, since the retained E-weights are exactly the distinct extremal weights $x(\lambda+ho)$, all of multiplicity one. The published Verma embedding criterion embeds the simple $\Delta(a)=L(a)$ in every standard in the block, so BGG reciprocity makes every standard multiplicity in $P(a)$ at least one. Since $P(a)$ is a summand of the once-each flag of $Q$, all these multiplicities are exactly one and the complementary summand has no flag factors, hence is zero.

items.title: Duflo–Joseph g-finite endomorphisms of every Verma module
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra and let $\mu$ be a highest weight. The action of
$U(\mathfrak g)$ on the Verma module $M(\mu)$ induces an algebra isomorphism
$$U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_\mu\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \bigl(\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}M(\mu)\bigr)^{\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak g\text{-finite}},$$
where the target is the locally finite part of the endomorphism algebra for
the adjoint action $x\mapsto[x,-]$. In particular
$\operatorname{Ann}M(\mu)=U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_\mu$. Moreover, for every
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module $E$,
$$\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M(\mu),E\otimes M(\mu))=\dim E_0,$$
and the action identifies each finite adjoint isotypic multiplicity with that
dimension.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 If $\mathfrak g=0$ then $U(\mathfrak g)=\mathbb C$, $M(\mu)=\mathbb C$ and everything is immediate; assume $\mathfrak g\neq0$, so $N=\dim\mathfrak n^->0$. By [F2] the Verma module $M(\mu)$ has finite length, so it contains a simple submodule; by [F2] every simple object is some $L(\eta)$ and the universal map $M(\eta)\to L(\eta)\hookrightarrow M(\mu)$ is injective; hence $M(\mu)$ contains $M(\eta)$ for a highest weight $\eta$. Writing $M(\mu)\cong U(\mathfrak n^-)$ by [F1], the submodule generated by the singular vector $p\,v_\mu$ is $U(\mathfrak n^-)p$: its embedding is right multiplication $u\mapsto up$ by a nonzero element $p\in U(\mathfrak n^-)$. [F1, F2]

1.2 Growth: the PBW filtration of $U(\mathfrak n^-)$ has $\dim F_nU(\mathfrak n^-)$ asymptotic to $n^N/N!$, while the quotient $U(\mathfrak n^-)/U(\mathfrak n^-)p$ has associated graded $S(\mathfrak n^-)/(\bar p)$ for the nonzero leading form $\bar p$ of $p$, so its Hilbert series is of the form $(1-t^d)/(1-t)^N$ and $\dim(U(\mathfrak n^-)/U(\mathfrak n^-)p)_{\le n}=O(n^{N-1})$; the same bound therefore holds for $M(\mu)/M(\eta)$ and, after tensoring by the finite-dimensional $E$, for $E\otimes(M(\mu)/M(\eta))$, because $\dim(E\otimes X)_{\le n}\le(\dim E)\dim X_{\le n}$. [F1, algebra]

1.3 The diagonal $U(\mathfrak n^-)$-action makes $E\otimes M(\mu)$ a free $U(\mathfrak n^-)$-module of rank $\dim E$, by [F5] applied to the identification $M(\mu)\cong U(\mathfrak n^-)$ of [F1]. In particular every nonzero vector $x$ of $E\otimes M(\mu)$ generates a copy $U(\mathfrak n^-)x$ of the domain $U(\mathfrak n^-)$, of growth $n^N$. [F1, F5]

1.4 The Hom space as a kernel: $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M(\mu),E\otimes M(\mu))$ is the space of $\mathfrak n^+$-invariants in the weight-$\mu$ space $(E\otimes M(\mu))_\mu$, i.e. the kernel of the finitely many raising maps $e_i:(E\otimes M(\mu))_\mu\to(E\otimes M(\mu))_{\mu+\alpha_i}$. This weight space has $\mu$-independent dimension $\sum_\nu\dim E_\nu\cdot\dim U(\mathfrak n^-)_{-\nu}$, and the matrices of the raising maps on fixed PBW bases have entries polynomial in $\mu$ by [F1]. [F1, algebra]

1.5 Simple-Verma case: if $M(\mu)=L(\mu)$ is simple, then $D\,M(\mu)=M(\mu)$ by [F4] and $M(\mu)=\nabla(\mu)$, and the tensor-hom adjunction plus [F4] give $$\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M(\mu),E\otimes M(\mu))=\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E^{*}\otimes M(\mu),M(\mu)),$$ which is the multiplicity of $\Delta(\mu)$ in the standard flag of $E^{*}\otimes M(\mu)$, namely $\dim E^{*}_0=\dim E_0$: by [F4] the flag factors are the $\Delta(\mu+\nu)$ with multiplicity $\dim E^{*}_\nu$, and $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta(\lambda),\nabla(\mu))=\mathbb C\delta_{\lambda\mu}$ while $\operatorname{Ext}^1$ vanishes. [F4, algebra]

2.1 Lower bound for all $\mu$: first the weights of simple Verma modules are Zariski dense. Indeed, if a Verma module has a nonzero proper submodule, choose a nonzero weight vector of minimal positive height $\beta\in Q^+\setminus\{0\}$ in it; every simple-root raising operator kills this vector, whose weight is $\mu-\beta$. The Casimir scalar on its cyclic highest-weight submodule equals that on $M(\mu)$, so [F7] gives $2(\mu+\rho,\beta)=(\beta,\beta)$. On the real root span the pairing is positive definite; this equality is impossible when $(\mu+\rho,\alpha_i)<0$ for every simple root. This nonempty real open chamber therefore consists of simple-Verma weights and is Zariski dense, since a complex polynomial vanishing on a real open set vanishes identically. The polynomial matrix of step 1.4 has a nonempty Zariski-open maximal-rank locus, which meets this dense set. At such an intersection step 1.5 gives kernel dimension $\dim E_0$; rank can only decrease at other weights, so $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M(\mu),E\otimes M(\mu))\ge\dim E_0$ for every $\mu$. [F1, F7, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]

2.2 Upper bound: the restriction map $$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M(\mu),E\otimes M(\mu))\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M(\eta),E\otimes M(\eta))$$ is injective. First, every $\varphi$ takes $M(\eta)$ into $E\otimes M(\eta)$: otherwise the composition with the projection $E\otimes(M(\mu)/M(\eta))$ would embed the simple $M(\eta)$, a copy of $U(\mathfrak n^-)$ of growth $n^N$ by step 1.1, into the module of growth $O(n^{N-1})$ from step 1.2, impossible. Second, if $\varphi\neq0$ killed $M(\eta)$, it would factor through $M(\mu)/M(\eta)$ and its nonzero image would contain, by step 1.3, a copy of the domain $U(\mathfrak n^-)$ of growth $n^N$, again contradicting step 1.2. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3]

2.3 Action injectivity setup: let $v$ be the highest vector of the simple Verma $M(\eta)\subseteq M(\mu)$ found in step 1.1 and pair $U(\mathfrak n^+)_\beta$ with $U(\mathfrak n^-)_{-\beta}$ by the Shapovalov form of $M(\eta)$, perfect in each weight by [F3]. For $0\neq x=\sum_\beta x_\beta$ in $U(\mathfrak n^-)\otimes U(\mathfrak n^+)$, choose a minimal $\beta$ with $x_\beta=\sum_i b_i\otimes a_i\neq0$ and a dual PBW vector $a_j^{*}\in U(\mathfrak n^-)_{-\beta}$ with $\langle a_i,a_j^{*}\rangle=\delta_{ij}$; acting on $a_j^{*}v$ all components of weight other than $\beta$ vanish by minimality and highest-weight support, and the surviving component is $b_jv$ for the index $j$ with $b_j\neq0$. Hence the composite $U(\mathfrak n^-)\otimes U(\mathfrak n^+)\to U(\mathfrak g)\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}M(\mu)$ is injective; its image has cumulative PBW growth bounded below by a positive multiple of $n^{2N}$. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Combining steps 1.5, 2.1 and 2.2, $$\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M(\mu),E\otimes M(\mu))=\dim E_0$$ for every highest weight $\mu$ and every finite-dimensional $E$; the same computation with $E$ replaced by its dual identifies the adjoint isotypic multiplicity in $U(\mathfrak g)$-modules with $\dim E_0$, by the freeness statement of [F6]. [F6, step 1.5, step 2.1, step 2.2]

3.2 Suppose the action had nonzero kernel $K$ in $U_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_\mu$. Then the associated graded $\operatorname{gr}(K)$ is a nonzero graded ideal of the domain $A$ of [F6], so it contains $Af$ for a nonzero homogeneous $f$; multiplication by $f$ is injective and the complete-intersection Hilbert series of $A$ gives $\dim(A/Af)_{\le n}=O(n^{2N-1})$. Consequently the image of $U(\mathfrak n^-)\otimes U(\mathfrak n^+)$ in $U_\chi$ has cumulative growth $O(n^{2N-1})$, contradicting the lower bound of step 2.3. Hence the action $U_\chi\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}M(\mu)$ is injective. [F6, step 2.3]

4.1 Surjectivity onto the locally finite part: the map of step 3.2 is $\mathfrak g$-equivariant for the adjoint actions, so it maps the $E$-isotypic component to the $E$-isotypic component for every finite-dimensional simple $E$. The source $E$-isotypic multiplicity is $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,U_\chi)=\dim E_0$ by [F6], and the target multiplicity is $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}M(\mu))=\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E\otimes M(\mu),M(\mu))=\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M(\mu),E^{*}\otimes M(\mu))=\dim E_0$ by step 3.1. An injective linear map between spaces of equal finite dimension is an isomorphism, so the action is an isomorphism onto each isotypic component, hence onto the locally finite part. [F6, step 3.1, step 3.2]

5.1 Since the kernel of $U(\mathfrak g)\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}M(\mu)$ is exactly $\operatorname{Ann}M(\mu)$ and the image of $U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_\mu$ lies in that kernel, steps 3.2 and 4.1 give both the algebra isomorphism and $\operatorname{Ann}M(\mu)=U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_\mu$; the multiplicity statement is step 3.1 read through the isomorphism. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the published category-$\mathcal O$ and invariant-theory suppliers. [F6, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Wall-crossing acts on standard modules by a two-step extension
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published items. Let
$\theta_s$ be the wall-crossing functor of
[[def-wall-crossing-functor-and-unit-counit]] attached to the simple reflection
$s$ in the regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$. For every $w\in W$ the
object $\theta_s\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ has a finite Verma flag with exactly two
factors, namely $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ and $\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)$, each with
multiplicity one; in the Grothendieck group
$$[\theta_s\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]=[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)].$$
Moreover $\theta_s$ is exact and preserves Verma-filtered objects with finite
Verma flags: if $X$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities
$(X:\Delta(v\cdot\lambda))$, then $\theta_sX$ has one with multiplicities
$(\theta_sX:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))=(X:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))+(X:\Delta(us\cdot\lambda))$,
and the same formula holds in $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$. The resulting flag is
not in general split; splitting is neither asserted nor used.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $\theta_s\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong T_{\mathrm{out}}\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ by the first clause of [F1], hence it has the two-factor finite Verma flag of the second clause of [F1] with factors $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ and $\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)$, each once; its class in $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$ is $[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)]$ by [F2]. [F1, F2]

2.1 Let $X$ be Verma-filtered with finite flag $0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$ and factors $\Delta(v_i\cdot\lambda)$. Exactness of $\theta_s$ by [F2] makes $0=\theta_sX_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\theta_sX_n=\theta_sX$ an increasing chain of subobjects, and each quotient $\theta_sX_i/\theta_sX_{i-1}\cong\theta_s(X_i/X_{i-1})\cong\theta_s\Delta(v_i\cdot\lambda)$ carries the two-factor flag of step 1.1; concatenating these two-step flags through the chain yields a finite Verma flag of $\theta_sX$ with factor multiplicities $(X:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))+(X:\Delta(us\cdot\lambda))$, where the independence of the flag [F2] makes the count well defined. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Summing the classes along the flag of step 2.1 gives $[\theta_sX]=\sum_i([\Delta(v_i\cdot\lambda)]+[\Delta(v_is\cdot\lambda)])=[X]+\sum_i[\Delta(v_is\cdot\lambda)]$, which is the stated formula $(\theta_sX:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))=(X:\Delta(u\cdot\lambda))+(X:\Delta(us\cdot\lambda))$; no splitting of the two-step extensions is used, and the claim extends to direct summands of $\theta_sX$ whenever they are Verma-filtered, by [F3]. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Base change, freeness and specialization in the deformed family
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. In the deformed family of
[[def-the-deformed-category-o-family-and-its-specializations]] with $T$ a
localization of $S=S(\mathfrak h)$ and $M,N\in\mathcal D_T(\lambda)$:

1. The canonical map
$$U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_ZT\longrightarrow\bigl(\operatorname{End}_T(M_T(\lambda))\bigr)^{\mathfrak g\text{-finite}},\qquad u\otimes t\longmapsto\bigl(m\mapsto u\cdot m\cdot t\bigr),$$
is an isomorphism of $T$-algebras, the superscript denoting the $\mathfrak g$-finite part for the adjoint action $X\cdot f=X\circ f-f\circ X$, and the center $Z=Z(U(\mathfrak g))$ acting on $T$ through the shifted Harish-Chandra isomorphism $\operatorname{HC}_\rho$ ([[thm-harish-chandra-isomorphism-for-the-center]]) followed by evaluation at $\lambda+\rho+\epsilon$ on the universal parameter $\epsilon$.
2. For finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-modules $E,F$, the $T$-module
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g\otimes T}(E\otimes M_T(\lambda),F\otimes M_T(\lambda))$
is free of rank $\dim(E\otimes F^{*})_0$, and the natural base-change map
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g\otimes T}(M,N)\otimes_T\kappa(\epsilon)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g\otimes\kappa(\epsilon)}(M\otimes_T\kappa(\epsilon),N\otimes_T\kappa(\epsilon))$$
is an isomorphism for every $\epsilon\in\operatorname{Spec}T$.
3. $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g\otimes T}(M,N)$ is locally free of finite rank over $T$.
4. If a $\mathfrak g\otimes R$-linear map of objects of $\mathcal D_R(\lambda)$ is an isomorphism on the special fiber at $0$, it is an isomorphism.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Work first over the polynomial ring $S$, before localizing. Put $G=F\otimes E^*$. Tensor-Hom adjunction identifies the stated tensor-object Hom module with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g\otimes S}(M_S(\lambda),G\otimes M_S(\lambda))$. A map is determined by a singular vector in the finite free deformed weight space of relative weight $\lambda$; the simple raising equations give a finite polynomial matrix $A$. The PBW model [F1] supplies the domain and codomain bases. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Every complex point of $\operatorname{Spec}S$ gives kernel dimension $\dim G_0$ by [F2], so $A$ has the same rank $s$ at every such point. Every $(s+1)$-minor therefore vanishes as a polynomial; the $s$-minors generate the unit ideal, because otherwise a maximal ideal containing them would be an evaluation ideal by [[cor-weak-nullstellensatz-algebraically-closed-coordinate-form]], contradicting rank $s$ there. On an open where an $s$-minor is invertible, row and column elimination gives $\operatorname{diag}(I_s,0)$. Thus the kernel is finite projective of rank $\dim G_0$ and commutes with arbitrary base change. This argument is over $S$, so it applies to every localization $T$, even one whose closed points are not complex evaluation points. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each finite-dimensional simple $L$, the adjoint $L$-multiplicity module of $U\otimes_ZS$ is $S\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(L,\mathcal H)$ by the harmonic decomposition [F3] and [F2]; it is finite free of rank $\dim L_0$. The action maps it to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(L,\operatorname{End}_S M_S(\lambda))$, which by tensor-Hom adjunction is the kernel from step 2.1 for $G=L^*$. At every complex point this map is an isomorphism by Duflo–Joseph [F2]. Its cokernel is finite and vanishes by local Nakayama at every maximal ideal of $S$; the resulting surjection splits onto the projective target, and its kernel, a projective module of rank zero, vanishes on each local free chart. Hence it is an isomorphism. Localizing gives the same result over $T$. Finite-dimensional complete reducibility decomposes every finite adjoint submodule, so these isotypic isomorphisms prove (1). [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For $G=F\otimes E^*$, tensor-Hom adjunction identifies the tensor-object Hom module with the adjoint $G^*$-multiplicity module of the endomorphism algebra in (1). Step 3.1 makes it free of rank $\dim G_0=\dim(E\otimes F^*)_0$; equality of the last dimensions follows by dualizing $G$. Step 2.1 proves its base-change assertion. Finite sums distribute over Hom, and for summands a Hom module is the image of the split idempotent $f\mapsto e_Nfe_M$ on an ambient Hom module. Such images are finite projective and commute with every base change. This proves (2) and (3) without claiming that arbitrary projective modules over arbitrary localizations are free. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Over the local ring $R$ at the origin, the deformed weight spaces of objects of $\mathcal D_R(\lambda)$ are finite projective, hence finite free: lift a residue basis, use Nakayama for a surjection from a free module, split it by projectivity, and apply Nakayama to the complementary kernel. A map whose residue fiber is an isomorphism has invertible determinant on each such weight space, so it has a weightwise inverse. The inverses commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action because the original map does. This proves (4). AC is inherited from the named suppliers. [F1, F3, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: The wall-crossing action on the Grothendieck group is multiplication by 1+s
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published items. In the
regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$ of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]] the
assignment
$$c\colon K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z[W],\qquad[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]\longmapsto w,$$
is an isomorphism of abelian groups, and for every simple reflection $s$ the
wall-crossing functor $\theta_s$ of
[[def-wall-crossing-functor-and-unit-counit]] satisfies
$$c\,[\theta_sX]=c\,[X]\cdot(1+s)\qquad\text{for all }X\in\mathcal O_\lambda,$$
right multiplication by $1+s$ in the integral group ring $\mathbb Z[W]$.
Consequently, for a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ one has
$$c\,[\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)]=(1+s_1)(1+s_2)\cdots(1+s_k),$$
the sum of all subexpression products with their actual multiplicities; its top
Bruhat term is $w$ once and all other terms have strictly smaller labels. With
the composition $\theta_{s_1}\cdots\theta_{s_k}$ instead, the factors are
multiplied in the reverse order.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The map $c$ is a well-defined homomorphism: by [F1] the classes of the standards are a $\mathbb Z$-basis indexed by the $|W|$ elements of $W$; sending the basis element $[\Delta(v\cdot\lambda)]$ to $v$ therefore extends uniquely to an isomorphism of free abelian groups of rank $|W|$. [F1]

2.1 On every Verma class the formula holds: $c[\theta_s\Delta(v\cdot\lambda)]=v+vs=v(1+s)=c[\Delta(v\cdot\lambda)]\cdot(1+s)$ by [F2], using that right multiplication by $s$ in $\mathbb Z[W]$ sends the basis element $v$ to $vs$. Since $\theta_s$ is exact by [F2] it induces an additive endomorphism of $K_0$; agreement on the standard basis [F1] gives $c[\theta_sX]=c[X](1+s)$ for all $X\in\mathcal O_\lambda$, and both sides are additive in $X$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Iterate step 2.1 along the word, applying the factors in the order in which they act: the composite $\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}$ applies $\theta_{s_1}$ first, so $c[\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)]=(((1+s_1))(1+s_2))\cdots(1+s_k)=(1+s_1)(1+s_2)\cdots(1+s_k)$; expanding the product gives the sum over all subwords $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_r}$, $i_1<\cdots<i_r$, of their products, with the multiplicity with which each product arises. The full subword contributes $w$ once; every proper subword has strictly smaller length, and its product is $\le w$ with smaller length, hence strictly smaller than $w$ in the Bruhat order by [F3]. Reversing the order of composition multiplies the factors in the reverse order, as recorded. [F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Wall-crossing compositions produce the projective with the top standard label
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a dominant regular integral representative
$\lambda$ and a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$, set
$\theta_{\underline w}=\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}$, so that the standards
follow right multiplication in word order. Then
$$\theta_{\underline w}\Delta(\lambda)\cong P(w\cdot\lambda)\oplus\bigoplus_{x<w}P(x\cdot\lambda)^{m_x},\qquad m_x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.$$
Its class is $(1+s_1)\cdots(1+s_k)$ under the standard class map, with actual
subexpression multiplicities. The BGG matrix satisfies
$(P(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=[\Delta(y\cdot\lambda):L(x\cdot\lambda)]$,
vanishes unless $y\le x$ in the Bruhat order, and has diagonal entries one.
Hence the top summand $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ occurs once and is the only summand
whose flag contains $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$; the remaining multiplicities are
determined by this triangular matrix and the product class. Consequently every
indecomposable projective is a summand of a word of wall crossings applied to
$\Delta(\lambda)$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The object $Y:=\theta_{\underline w}\Delta(\lambda)$ is projective by [F1], and the block has finite-dimensional Hom spaces and finite decompositions, so $Y\cong\bigoplus_xP(x\cdot\lambda)^{m_x}$ with nonnegative multiplicities; its standard-flag multiplicities are read from its class in [F2], and every standard factor has a label $\le w$. [F1, F2]

2.1 No summand $P(x\cdot\lambda)$ with $x\not\le w$ occurs: the diagonal entry of the BGG matrix gives $(P(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))=1$ by [F3], so such a summand would contribute a standard factor $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ to $Y$ with $x\not\le w$, contradicting step 1.1. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 The full subexpression contributes $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ with multiplicity one to the product class, and no other summand $P(x\cdot\lambda)$ with $x\le w$, $x\neq w$ contributes to the multiplicity of $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$: $(P(x\cdot\lambda):\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))\neq0$ forces $w\le x$ by [F3], so with $x\le w$ it forces $x=w$. Hence $m_w=1$, and the only summand whose flag contains $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ is $P(w\cdot\lambda)$. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 The remaining multiplicities $m_x$, $x<w$, are determined recursively from the product class: the coefficient of $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ in the class of $Y$ equals $m_x+\sum_{x<z}m_z(P(z\cdot\lambda):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))$, whose second term involves only strictly larger labels already determined; solving downward in the finite Bruhat order gives all $m_x$. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Every indecomposable projective is a summand of such a word: the decomposition of step 1.1 with diagonal support realizes each $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ as a summand of $\theta_{\underline w}\Delta(\lambda)$ for any reduced word $w$, which is the stated generation statement. [step 3.1] ∎

items.title: Lifting of indecomposable projectives to the deformed family
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be dominant regular integral,
$R=S(\mathfrak h)_{(0)}$ the localization at the origin, and use the selected
component $\mathcal D_R^{[\lambda]}(\lambda)$ of the tensor-generated deformed
family of [[def-the-deformed-category-o-family-and-its-specializations]]. For
every $x\in W$ there is a projective $P_R(x,\lambda)$ in the deformed
$\lambda$-block whose residue fiber is $P(x\cdot\lambda)$; it is unique up to
isomorphism, and every indecomposable of this selected tensor component is one
of these lifts. Each lift has a finite deformed Verma flag with the same
multiplicities as its closed fiber. More generally, a finite projective in this
block is a direct summand of a finite sum of truncated induced projectives
representing relative weight spaces; for every map of deformation algebras
$R\to R'$ its base change is projective in the corresponding truncated category
and
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_R}(P,N)\otimes_RR'\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_{R'}}(P\otimes_RR',N\otimes_RR').$$
For a finite Verma-filtered target $N$ this Hom module is finite free over
local $R$. A $\mathfrak g\otimes R$-linear map between such finite
projective/Verma-filtered objects whose residue fiber is an isomorphism is
itself an isomorphism, weight by weight. For a dot-dominant integral target
$\nu$, including singular $\nu$, the same local projective construction gives
all lifts in its deformed block, with labels the distinct cosets $W/W_\nu$;
these lifts belong to the target component $\mathcal D_R^{[\nu]}(\lambda)$ of a
regular-source tensor family. It is neither necessary nor asserted that the
singular Verma itself generates every target projective, and the other central
components of the full tensor family are not claimed to have only these
indecomposables.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** construct relative truncated weight projectives, then lift both maps of an actual split inclusion; no idempotent-lifting assumption on $R$ is used.

1.1 Here is the ambient category used for the truncated assertions. For a deformation algebra $T$, its objects are finitely generated $U(\mathfrak g)\otimes T$-modules which are direct sums of relative weight spaces $N^\xi=\{n:hn=(\xi(h)+\tau(h))n\text{ for all }h\in\mathfrak h\}$, have finite $T$-modules as weight spaces, and have weights in a finite union of downward root cones. Morphisms preserve those weight spaces. The full subcategory $\mathcal O_T^{\le\Lambda}$ has weights $\xi\le\Lambda$ in one root-lattice coset; for a finite union of cosets use one bound in each coset. Kernels, cokernels and extensions remain in this category: weight decomposition makes weight spaces exact, the enveloping algebra over Noetherian $R$ is Noetherian by PBW, and positive-root action is locally nilpotent because only finitely many weights above a fixed weight occur. For arbitrary $R'$ the representing construction below uses the analogous category of relative weight modules, without requiring kernels of finitely generated objects to be finitely generated. Thus every projectivity/base-change assertion has a specified ambient category, distinct from the additive tensor family. [F1, algebra]

1.2 A direct summand of a finite deformed Verma-filtered object over $R$ again has a deformed Verma flag. To see this, choose a maximal highest-weight label $\eta$ of its flag. Positive-root action above $\eta$ vanishes, so the full $\eta$-weight space consists of highest-weight vectors. Successive examination of the flag gives an injection $\Delta_R(\eta)\otimes_R X^\eta\to X$ with Verma-filtered quotient: in a factor of another label no weight $\eta$ occurs, and a factor of label $\eta$ contributes its free highest-weight line; lifting that line is unobstructed since there is no weight strictly above $\eta$. PBW verifies injectivity and the quotient assertion along the finite flag. This submodule is canonical and preserved by every endomorphism of $X$. An idempotent therefore splits its finite free coefficient space into finite free images over local $R$, and induces an idempotent on the quotient. Induction on flag length supplies flags on both summands. Specialization of such a flag is exact and preserves each multiplicity, since all the flag factors and their weight spaces are $R$-free. [F1, F4, algebra]

2.1 Fix $\xi\le\Lambda$. In $U(\mathfrak b)\otimes T$, quotient by the left ideal generated by $h-\xi(h)-\tau(h)$ and by every positive PBW monomial of weight $\beta$ for which $\xi+\beta\not\le\Lambda$. The latter monomials form a positive left ideal since adding a positive root cannot restore the inequality. Call the resulting $\mathfrak b$-module $B_T^\Lambda(\xi)$, and put $Q_T^\Lambda(\xi)=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}B_T^\Lambda(\xi)$. PBW gives a finite $T$-basis of the retained positive monomials: the allowed $\beta$ have bounded simple-root coefficients. Ordering them by decreasing height gives a $\mathfrak b$-stable filtration, refined within each weight, with rank-one quotients of weights $\xi+\beta+\tau$. Exact induction by PBW gives a finite deformed Verma flag on $Q_T^\Lambda(\xi)$, and all its weights are $\le\Lambda$. Evaluation at the cyclic generator gives $\operatorname{Hom}(Q_T^\Lambda(\xi),N)=N^\xi$ for $N\in\mathcal O_T^{\le\Lambda}$: the excluded monomials kill every vector of that weight, and those are precisely the defining relations. The weight functor is exact, so $Q_T^\Lambda(\xi)$ is projective. This description commutes with every map $T\to T'$, as does its Hom functor whenever $N$ is base changed, because $(N\otimes_TT')^\xi=N^\xi\otimes_TT'$ in the specified relative-weight decomposition. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Every finitely generated projective in this truncated category is a direct summand of a finite sum of these $Q$'s. Indeed choose finitely many homogeneous generators of the projective; the corresponding evaluations give a surjection from that sum, and projectivity splits it. Consequently its Hom functor commutes with arbitrary algebra base change, by restricting the weight-space isomorphisms of step 2.1 to the image of its split idempotent. For a Verma-filtered target all weight spaces are finite free over $R$, since each successive weight-space quotient is finite free and the finite extensions split as $R$-modules. Hom from a finite sum of $Q$'s is therefore finite free, and Hom from its summand is finite projective, hence finite free over local $R$: lift a residue basis, split the resulting Nakayama surjection, and apply Nakayama to its kernel. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Apply the projectors of [F3] to $Q_R^\Lambda(\xi)$ to select the required block, with $\Lambda$ a dominant bound. Its residue is an ordinary projective and decomposes into projective covers. Evaluation into a simple gives $\operatorname{Hom}(Q_k^\Lambda(\xi),L(\eta))=L(\eta)^\xi$, so a summand $P(\eta)$ can occur only when $\eta\ge\xi$, and $P(\xi)$ occurs once if $\xi$ is a highest-weight label. Order the finite orbit by decreasing highest weight. Suppose all higher $P_R(\eta)$ have already been constructed. Let $H_R$ be their sum with the multiplicities in the actual decomposition of the residue of the selected $Q$. Over $k$ choose the split inclusion $i_0:H_k\to Q_k$ and projection $p_0:Q_k\to H_k$. Step 3.1 lifts both to $i,p$ over $R$, because both sources are already projective. The composite $pi$ is the identity modulo $\mathfrak m$, hence invertible weight by weight by Nakayama. Replace $p$ by $(pi)^{-1}p$; then $pi=1$ and $Q_R=i(H_R)\oplus\ker p$ is an actual split decomposition. The complement is projective, has a Verma flag by step 1.2, and has residue $P(\xi)$. This constructs $P_R(\xi)$ recursively, with its asserted multiplicities. The first label needs no subtraction. [F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, step 1.2, construct]

5.1 If $P_R$ and $P'_R$ are two such lifts, lift an ordinary isomorphism and its inverse using step 3.1 for both projective sources. Their composites are identity on the residue and hence are isomorphisms weight by weight; adjusting either map gives an isomorphism $P_R\cong P'_R$. This proves uniqueness by actual maps, rather than by a Grothendieck class. A nonzero direct summand of a lift has a nonzero residue: its finite projective weight spaces cannot all have zero residue by Nakayama. Since the residue cover is indecomposable, each lift is indecomposable. More generally lift the two splitting maps for the complete residue decomposition of any finite Verma-filtered projective; the same composite-inverse construction identifies it with the sum of the corresponding lifts. [F2, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The abstract lifts belong to the tensor-generated family without presuming its deformed projectivity. Each selected deformed wall word has a Verma flag with labels in $W\cdot\lambda$, hence weights $\le\lambda$, and its residue is an ordinary projective by exact tensor biadjunction and block projection. Decompose that residue into its actual projective covers, and form the corresponding sum $H_R$ of the abstract lifts of step 4.1, all constructed in $\mathcal O_R^{\le\lambda}$. The residue isomorphism $H_k\to X_k$ lifts to $H_R\to X_R$ by step 3.1, whose source is already a truncated projective; the target need not yet be known projective. Both objects have finite free weight spaces, so [F4] makes this map an isomorphism. Thus the deformed word is an actual direct sum of abstract lifts; whenever its residue contains $P(x\cdot\lambda)$, that lift is a tensor-family summand. The ordinary covering statement [F2] supplies such a word for every $x$. Exactly the same source-projective argument applies to any selected tensor object: its residue is projective, its selected flag labels lie in $W\cdot\lambda$, and the lifted residue decomposition map is invertible. Hence every such object is a sum of these lifts and all its indecomposables are exactly the stated ones. This proves deformed projectivity by comparison with the representing projectives. [F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

6.2 Steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the arbitrary-base-change Hom isomorphism and projectivity after base change for every finite truncated projective, including each selected lift. A map between the projective/Verma-filtered objects appearing here has finite free source and target weight spaces; if its residue is an isomorphism, the matrix on each weight space has determinant a unit and is invertible. The weightwise inverses commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action since the original map does, so the map is an isomorphism. This verifies all the base-change, freeness and weightwise assertions in the Statement. [F4, step 3.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 For a singular dot-dominant target $\nu$, steps 1.1--5.1 apply to its finite orbit of distinct weights, indexed by $W/W_\nu$, with bound $\nu$. Onto translation sends a regular standard with label $y$ to the singular standard with label $yW_\nu$, once: the dominant norm equality says $x^{-1}yv\in W_\nu v$, hence $xu=yu$, where $u=\nu+\rho$ and $v=\lambda+\rho$; it does not say that $W_\nu v$ is a singleton. In particular every singular Verma is an onto-translated regular Verma. Every singular simple is therefore a quotient of an onto-translated regular projective, by exactness and the regular projective cover. Onto translation is ordinarily projective-preserving by biadjunction, so its decomposition contains that singular simple's projective cover. Apply its deformed tensor-and-projector construction to the regular lifts already in the family. The resulting object has a deformed singular Verma flag, weights $\le\nu$, and projective ordinary residue. As in step 6.1, lift a residue isomorphism from the sum of its already constructed abstract singular truncated-projective lifts to this object, using step 3.1 for that source, and invert it weightwise by [F4]. Thus each abstract singular lift is a summand of a regular-source tensor-family object. Conversely every selected singular tensor object has projective residue and the same argument identifies it with the sum of its singular lifts. This proves the target-component assertion over the original polynomial local ring $R$, with no supposition that the singular Verma generates every projective. [F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Indecomposable projective functors are indexed by the Weyl group
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral block with dominant
representative $\lambda$:

1. Projective functors form a Krull-Schmidt category.
2. Their indecomposables are indexed by $W$, with $\Theta_w$ characterized by
$\Theta_w\Delta(\lambda)\cong P(w\cdot\lambda)$. For a reduced word
$w=s_1\cdots s_k$, the functor $\Theta_w$ is a multiplicity-one summand of
$\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}$, and every other indecomposable summand has a
label $x<w$. In particular every indecomposable projective functor is generated
as a summand by wall crossings.
3. Two projective functors are naturally equivalent exactly when their induced
operators on the Grothendieck group agree.

The characterization concerns evaluation on the dominant projective Verma; no
faithfulness of that evaluation on all natural maps of arbitrary
endofunctors is asserted.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $\mathcal A$ be the class of projective functors and evaluate a natural transformation $\alpha$ at $\Delta(\lambda)$. For ambient tensor functors, lift the finite equivariant coefficient map in [F1] to $U$. Its tensor coefficients act on every module by the same formula, yielding a natural $\mathfrak g$-map. For projected functors, extend a map between projected evaluations by inclusion and projection to the ambient tensors, lift it there, then project on the output and include on the input. The same inclusion/retraction procedure handles functor summands. Thus evaluation is surjective on Hom spaces. [F1]

2.1 The evaluation kernel is nilpotent. If $\alpha$ vanishes on $\Delta(\lambda)$, then by exactness and naturality it vanishes on every standard, since each standard embeds in $\Delta(\lambda)$ by [F2] and exactness preserves the embedding; on a fixed projective generator with a finite Verma flag of length $k$, vanishing on the standard factors strictly lowers the flag, so a composition of $k$ such maps is zero. Hence $\ker$ is a nilpotent ideal on every finite additive functor sum. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Idempotents lift across a nilpotent ideal (if $e^2-e=d$ lies in a nilpotent ideal, replace $e$ by $e+(1-2e)d$; its idempotent error lies in the square of the previous error ideal, so finitely many repetitions give an idempotent) and an element $1+$nilpotent is invertible by a finite geometric series; hence decompositions and isomorphism classes of projective functors coincide with those of their evaluations at $\Delta(\lambda)$, and the endomorphism algebra of an indecomposable is local exactly when its evaluation is. Hom spaces are finite-dimensional for a separate reason: a natural transformation between right-exact functors is determined by its value on a finite projective generator $H=\bigoplus_xP(x\cdot\lambda)$, since every object has a finite presentation by sums of $H$. Its component is a member of the finite-dimensional space $\operatorname{Hom}(FH,F'H)$ (maps are determined by images of finitely many weight-homogeneous generators into finite-dimensional weight spaces). Thus the functor category has finite-dimensional endomorphism algebras and split idempotents. Nilpotent-kernel lifting matches its indecomposable decompositions to those of the evaluations, proving Krull–Schmidt. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F3] the wall word $\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}$ evaluated at $\Delta(\lambda)$ has the decompositions $P(w\cdot\lambda)\oplus\bigoplus_{x<w}P(x\cdot\lambda)^{m_x}$; by step 3.1 this decomposition lifts uniquely to a decomposition of the functor, producing $\Theta_w$ with $\Theta_w\Delta(\lambda)\cong P(w\cdot\lambda)$ and with all other summands labelled $x<w$; conversely every indecomposable projective functor is a summand of such a word, so the labels $w\in W$ exhaust the indecomposables. This proves (1) and (2). [F3, step 3.1]

5.1 If two projective functors have the same class operator on $K_0$, then their evaluations at $\Delta(\lambda)$ are projectives with the same class; by the unitriangular BGG matrix [F4] their indecomposable decompositions agree, so the evaluations are isomorphic, and by step 3.1 the functors are naturally equivalent; the converse is formal. This proves (3). [F4, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: The central action on the deformed antidominant projective
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be dominant regular integral,
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$, $R=S_{(0)}$, and $P_R=P_R(w_0,\lambda)$ the deformed
antidominant projective. Write $\operatorname{HC}_\rho\colon Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to S^W$
for the published shifted Harish-Chandra isomorphism,
$\sigma_\lambda(f)(\epsilon)=f(\lambda+\rho+\epsilon)$, and define
$$a_\lambda\colon Z\otimes_{\mathbb C}R\longrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R,\qquad z\otimes r\longmapsto\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))\otimes r.$$
Then $a_\lambda$ and the action map $Z\otimes R\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)$
are surjective and have the same kernel, inducing a canonical $R$-algebra
isomorphism
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)\cong R\otimes_{R^W}R.$$
On a generic Verma constituent of highest weight $x\cdot\lambda+\epsilon$, $z$
acts by the scalar
$\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)(x(\lambda+\rho)+\epsilon)=\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))(x^{-1}\epsilon)$;
these scalars vary with $x$, and the center need not act by a single scalar on
$P_R$. After tensoring the right $R$ factor with the residue field at $0$, the
endomorphism algebra becomes $C=S/(S^W_+S)$. More generally, for dot-dominant
integral $\nu$ the corresponding algebra is $R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R$, where
$W_\nu$ is the dot stabilizer. Translation out of that facet identifies the
singular antidominant projective with the regular one; under these shifted
Harish-Chandra identifications, its induced endomorphism map is the inclusion
$R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R\hookrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The block at $\eta=-\rho$ has a single highest weight in $W\cdot\eta\cap(\eta-Q^+)=\{\eta\}$, so $M(\eta)=L(\eta)$ is simple, its projective cover has a Verma flag whose single factor is $L(\eta)$ by BGG reciprocity, hence equals $L(\eta)$ and $L(\eta)$ is projective; with a single simple object and enough projectives the block is semisimple, so $L(\eta)$ is injective as well, and the well-definedness part of [F6] then supplies the object $Q=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}(E\otimes L(\eta))$, which is projective and injective and has a Verma flag with the factors $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$, $x\in W$, once each, together with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(Q,L(a))\cong\mathbb C$ and a split embedding $P(a)\hookrightarrow Q$; the same construction with the distinct extremal weights $Wv=W/W_\nu$ gives the singular once-each flag. [F1, F6]

1.2 Let $p$ be a height-one prime of $R$, $T=R_p$, $k=\operatorname{Frac}(R/p)$, and let $\tau$ be the tautological parameter of the deformed family; the residual central characters are the $W$-classes of the points $xv+\tau$, $x\in W$, and $\chi_{xv+\tau}=\chi_{yv+\tau}$ over $k$ forces $xv+\tau=w(yv+\tau)$ for some $w$ by [F1] and finite interpolation, so comparing the constant and linear parts modulo $p$ gives $xv=wyv$ and $w\tau=\tau$ in $k$; a nonidentity $w$ fixing the generic point of the divisor $p$ fixes a hyperplane, hence is the orthogonal reflection in that hyperplane. That hyperplane must be a root hyperplane: otherwise it contains a root-regular real point, whose open chamber would be stabilized by $w$, contradicting [[thm-the-weyl-group-acts-simply-transitively-on-weyl-chambers]]. Thus $p$ is the root prime $\langle\tau,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ for that root; therefore at every nonroot prime all residual characters are pairwise distinct, while at the root prime the equal-character classes are exactly the pairs $\{x,s_\alpha x\}$ together with singleton classes wherever $s_\alpha xv=xv$, which occurs in the singular case. [F1, F8, algebra]

1.3 At a root divisor, isolate one two-element residual character class by CRT. Write its upper and lower weights $A=a+\tau$ and $B=b+\tau$, where $b=s_\alpha\cdot a=a-n\alpha$ and $n=\langle a+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle>0$. Over $k=\operatorname{Frac}(R/p)$, a singular vector of weight $A-\gamma$ must satisfy the Casimir equation $2(A+\rho,\gamma)=(\gamma,\gamma)$. Its parameter term vanishes identically on the divisor only if $\gamma$ is a multiple of $\alpha$, and its constant term then forces $\gamma=n\alpha$. The Shapovalov determinant on that weight has valuation one: only its $(\alpha,n)$ factor vanishes, with exponent $K(0)=1$, so its residue radical has dimension one there. A nonzero radical has a highest-weight vector, by choosing minimal root height among its nonzero weight spaces; it is therefore generated initially by that one-dimensional $B$-weight space. The same Casimir equation for $B$ has no solution with positive $\gamma$, so $M(B)$ is simple. Its highest vector gives an injected $M(B)\to M(A)$: the induced map is injective because its simple source is nonzero. Any nonzero quotient of the radical by this image would again have a highest-weight vector; the equation forces weight $B$, but its $B$-space is zero. Thus $\operatorname{Rad}M(A)=M(B)$ and $M(A)$ has length two. This proves the required divisor-field classification directly; no closed-point or complex-only classification is substituted for it. [F2, F3, algebra]

1.4 Let $u=\nu+\rho$ be dominant with $H=\operatorname{Stab}(u)$, and $v=\lambda+\rho$ regular dominant. For onto translation, a retained factor satisfies $yv+\gamma=xu$. The norm bound and dominant-distance inequality force equality $|\gamma|=|u-v|$ and $x^{-1}yv\in Hv$; because $v$ is regular this means $x^{-1}y\in H$, hence $xu=yu$. Thus the retained standard is $\Delta(y\cdot\nu)$ once. This uses the coset condition, not the false assertion $Hv=\{v\}$. For return translation the retained labels are $x\in yH$, each extremal weight once. The conclusion is a Verma flag with factors $\Delta(yh\cdot\lambda)$ for $h\in H$, not a direct sum. The same calculation applies to the deformed tensor flags, with the common parameter $\tau$ retained. [F4, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 Every standard $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ contains $L(a)$ as a composition factor: $a$ is the minimal weight of $W\cdot a$, so the Verma embedding criterion gives a nonzero, hence injective, map $M(a)=L(a)\to\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$, and BGG reciprocity gives $(P(a):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))=[\Delta(x\cdot\lambda):L(a)]\ge1$, while $(P(a):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))\le(Q:\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))=1$ because $P(a)$ is a summand of $Q$; hence all multiplicities equal one, the complementary summand of $P(a)$ in $Q$ has flag length zero, and $Q=P(a)$; the argument applies verbatim to a dot-dominant singular $\nu$ with $Wv$ replaced by $W/W_\nu$. [F6, step 1.1]

2.2 Put $K=\operatorname{Frac}R$ and $B=R\otimes_{R^W}R$. Localization of the free invariant/harmonic decomposition in [F8] makes it finite free of rank $|W|$ over the right $R$. Evaluation embeds it into $K^W$ by $f\otimes r\mapsto(f(x^{-1}\tau)r)_x$: generically the orbit has $|W|$ distinct points, interpolation makes this map surjective after tensoring with $K$, and freeness makes it injective over $R$. At a nonroot height-one prime, residual orbit points are distinct and CRT gives $B_T=T^W$. At a root prime CRT isolates the pairs from step 1.2. Every pair evaluation is congruent modulo the root uniformizer $\alpha=\langle\tau,\alpha^\vee\rangle$. Choose a linear $f$ for which the two values differ by a unit times $\alpha$; subtract its lower value and multiply by the pair projector to obtain $(\alpha,0)$. Together with the pair identity this generates exactly the congruence order $\{(u,v)\in T^2:u-v\in\alpha T\}$. For a singular stabilizer $H=W_\nu$, Reynolds averaging on the first factor identifies $B^H=R^H\otimes_{R^W}R$. It is finite projective over right $R$ as a split summand of $B$, hence free since $R$ is local; its generic rank is $|W/H|$. The same pair and singleton orders, now on cosets, follow by taking the $H$-fixed tuples. [F8, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Localize $P_R$ to $T=R_p$. Its full flag still has $|W|$ factors; CRT in the finitely many residual central characters splits it into pair components and singleton components. Write $P_{T,\{A,B\}}$ for one pair summand. Only this summand has the two factors $\Delta_T(A)$ and $\Delta_T(B)$ once. Maximal-weight generation gives $0\to\Delta_T(A)\to P_{T,\{A,B\}}\to\Delta_T(B)\to0$. It is projective in its character component by base change and splitting. The residual extension cannot split: otherwise its direct summand $M(B)$ would be projective, but duality applied to the nonsplit length-two $M(A)$ yields a nonsplit extension $0\to L(A)\to D M(A)\to L(B)=M(B)\to0$, contradicting projectivity. At a singleton the summand has a single standard. The identical argument applies to the singular once-each flag, with root-fixed labels giving singletons. Over the fraction field all standard characters are distinct and all Vermas are simple by the Shapovalov determinant; hence each component is its indicated standard and the generic endomorphism algebra is the tuple algebra. [F3, F5, F7, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Translation out carries $P_R^\nu$ to a regular projective by the exact tensor biadjunction and the actual central projectors. Its flag contains every regular standard once by steps 2.1 and 1.4. On the closed fiber, onto translation takes the regular antidominant simple Verma to the singular antidominant simple Verma, so adjunction gives a one-dimensional Hom from the return projective to the regular antidominant simple. Its regular antidominant cover splits off; both have every standard once, so the complement has zero flag and vanishes. Hom base change and the two-map lifting argument of [F7] now give $T_{\mathrm{out}}P_R^\nu\cong P_R^\lambda$. Any two choices induce the same endomorphism map after identification, since the endomorphism algebra is commutative (as will follow from its generic tuple embedding). [F6, F7, step 2.1, step 1.4, algebra]

4.1 Any endomorphism $f$ of the isolated pair $P_{T,\{A,B\}}$ preserves $\Delta_T(A)$ and acts by scalars $u_a$ on $\Delta_T(A)$ and $u_b$ on $\Delta_T(B)$; if $u_a-u_b$ were a unit modulo $p$, the residual projector $(f-u_b)/(u_a-u_b)$, polynomial in $f$ since $(f-u_a)(f-u_b)=0$ on the two-step flag, would split the nonsplit residual extension of step 3.1, so $u_a\equiv u_b$ modulo $\tau(\alpha^\vee)$ and $\operatorname{End}(P_{T,\{A,B\}})$ lies in the congruence order; the central Casimir element acts on the two generic standards by $(A,A+2\rho)$ and $(B,B+2\rho)$, eigenvalues differing by $2n(\alpha,\tau)=n(\alpha,\alpha)\langle\tau,\alpha^\vee\rangle$, a unit times the uniformizer, so the Casimir minus the lower eigenvalue gives the pair $(\tau(\alpha^\vee),0)$ and together with the identity generates the full congruence order, both generators being central actions; on singleton classes the order is $T$, generated by the identity. [F1, F2, step 3.1]

5.1 The generic tuple embeddings place $\operatorname{End}(P_R)$ and $B$ (or $\operatorname{End}(P_R^\nu)$ and $B^H$) inside the same tuple algebra. Both are finite free right-$R$ modules: for End this is [F7], for $B^H$ it is Reynolds averaging in step 2.2. Steps 3.1, 2.2 and 4.1 identify their localizations at each height-one prime, pair by pair, including the singular singletons. A finite free $R$-lattice equals the intersection of its height-one localizations inside its fraction-field span. Indeed $R$ is a localization of a polynomial UFD, and $R=\bigcap_{\operatorname{ht}p=1}R_p$: a reduced fractional denominator outside $R$ has a nonunit irreducible factor detected at its prime; applying this coefficientwise to any free lattice basis proves the lattice assertion. Thus the two lattices are equal and yield the asserted algebra identification. This does not yet assert that the global central image is saturated; its surjectivity is established separately below. [F7, F8, step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 For a dominant shifted weight $u$ with stabilizer $H$, the closed right fiber of $B^H$ is $C^H$, because averaging commutes with quotienting by the right maximal ideal. Choose $N$ above the largest ordinary polynomial degree in $C$, and choose an $H$-invariant representative $h(\tau)$ of any prescribed class in $C^H$ by averaging. Prescribe the jet $h(X-u)$ of order $N$ at $u$, and zero jets at the other distinct points in $Wu$. Polynomial CRT produces $q$ with those jets. Then $p(X)=|H|^{-1}\sum_{w\in W}q(w^{-1}X)$ is $W$-invariant. At $X=u+\tau$, precisely the $w\in H$ terms contribute, and their jets equal $h(w^{-1}\tau)=h(\tau)$; the other terms vanish to order $N$. Hence $p(u+\tau)\equiv h(\tau)\pmod{(\tau)^N}$, whose image in $C$ is the prescribed class. In the regular case take $u=v$ and $H=1$; in the singular case take the actual singular $u$, never regular $v$. By [F1], $p=\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)$ for a central element $z$. [F1, F8, F9, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 The image of $a_\lambda$ is an $R$-submodule of the finite free target $B$ respectively $B^H$ whose cokernel is finitely generated and has zero closed fiber by step 6.1; Nakayama over the local ring $R$ makes the cokernel zero, so $a_\lambda$ is surjective, and the action map $Z\otimes R\to\operatorname{End}(P_R)$ is surjective with it under the identification of step 5.1. [F7, step 5.1, step 6.1]

8.1 Under the tuple identification, $z\otimes r$ acts on the generic constituent of highest weight $x\cdot\lambda+\tau$ by the scalar $\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)(x(\lambda+\rho)+\tau)r=\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))(x^{-1}\tau)r$, these scalars vary with $x$, and the injective tuple embedding shows that an element of $Z\otimes R$ acts by zero if and only if its image in $B$ respectively $B^H$ is zero; hence the action map and $a_\lambda$ have the same kernel and induce the displayed isomorphism, while, writing $k=R/\mathfrak m=\mathbb C$ for the residue field (distinct from the coinvariant algebra $C$), tensoring the right factor with $k$ gives $(R\otimes_{R^W}R)\otimes_R k\cong R/(R^W_+R)=C$ respectively $(R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R)\otimes_R k\cong C^{W_\nu}$. [F1, step 5.1, step 7.1]

9.1 On generic constituents translation out repeats the scalar attached to a coset $yH$ on every branch $yh$, so under the identifications of steps 5.1 and 8.1 the map $\operatorname{End}(P_R^\nu)\to\operatorname{End}(T_{\mathrm{out}}P_R^\nu)=\operatorname{End}(P_R^\lambda)$ induced by the translation identification of step 3.2 is the inclusion $R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R\hookrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R$; this holds uniformly across the facet, including the regular case $W_\nu=\{1\}$, where it is the identity. [step 3.2, step 5.1, step 8.1] ∎

items.title: The endomorphisms of the antidominant projective form the coinvariant algebra
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be finite-dimensional complex
semisimple, $\lambda$ the dominant regular integral representative of a block
and $\mathcal O_\lambda$ its block with antidominant weight $w_0\cdot\lambda$.
Let $C$ be the coinvariant algebra of
[[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]] for the Cartan
reflection representation, with its grading fixed there. Then:

(1) the natural maps $Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to C$ (Harish-Chandra isomorphism,
shifted by $\lambda+\rho$ in the published $\operatorname{HC}_\rho$ convention,
followed by the quotient map $\rho$) and $Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$
(multiplication) are surjective with the same kernel;

(2) consequently the multiplication map induces a canonical algebra isomorphism
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P(w_0\cdot\lambda)\ \cong\ C,$$
identifying $C$ with the endomorphism ring of the antidominant projective,
canonically and independently of the choice of projective cover inside its
isomorphism class;

(3) the grading on the right-hand side is the internal grading of the
coinvariant algebra; no graded lift of category $\mathcal O$ is asserted or
used.

This is Soergel's Endomorphismensatz [Soe90, Theorem 7], in the regular integral
case; the companion general form for singular blocks replaces $C$ by the
invariants $C^{W_\lambda}$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1] the multiplication map $Z\otimes R\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)$ is surjective, has the same kernel as $a_\lambda$, and makes the following diagram commute: $Z\otimes R\xrightarrow{\ a_\lambda\ }R\otimes_{R^W}R\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)$. [F1]

1.2 Specializing the right factor along $R\to\mathbb C$ (the residue field at $0$) carries algebra isomorphisms to algebra isomorphisms, and [F2] identifies $\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)\otimes_R\mathbb C\cong\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}(P_R\otimes_R\mathbb C)=\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$, while the target specializes to $(R\otimes_{R^W}R)\otimes_R\mathbb C\cong R/(S\,S^W_+)=C$, and $a_\lambda$ specializes to the map sending $z$ to the class of $\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)(\lambda+\rho+\tau)$. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Specializing the isomorphism of step 1.1 therefore gives the canonical algebra isomorphism $\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P(w_0\cdot\lambda)\cong C$, induced by the multiplication action alone and hence independent of the chosen projective cover up to the canonical identification; the specialized multiplication map is the shifted Harish-Chandra composite $z\mapsto\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)(\lambda+\rho+\tau)$ followed by the quotient map $R\to C$, it is surjective, and the commutative diagram identifies its kernel with that of the multiplication map. Tensoring need not preserve kernels; no exactness of residue-field tensoring is used. [F1, F3, step 1.2]

3.1 The grading in (3) is the internal grading of $C$ transported along the isomorphism of step 2.1; no $\mathbb Z$-grading of category-$\mathcal O$ objects or of the Hom spaces is used; for a singular dominant integral $\lambda$ the same specialization of the central-action lemma gives $\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P\cong C^{W_\lambda}$, replacing the coinvariant algebra by its invariants. [F1, F4, step 2.1] ∎

items.title: Soergel's Struktursatz: the functor V is fully faithful on projectives
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal O_\lambda$ be a regular integral block
with antidominant projective $P=P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ and Soergel functor
$V=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,-)$, and let $C$ be the coinvariant
algebra, identified with $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)$ by
[[thm-endomorphisms-of-the-antidominant-projective-are-the-coinvariant-algebra]],
so that $V$ takes values in $C$-modules. Then for every $M\in\mathcal O_\lambda$
and every projective $Q\in\mathcal O_\lambda$ the canonical map
$$V\colon \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_\lambda}(M,Q)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{C\text{-mod}}(VM,VQ)$$
is an isomorphism. In particular $V$ is fully faithful on the full subcategory
of projective objects of the block, and it is faithful on all of
$\mathcal O_\lambda$ after passing to the quotient by the Serre subcategory of
objects killed by $V$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; the annihilator argument follows Soergel, §2.3, Lemma 6 and Struktursatz 9 (preprint pp. 15–16).

1.1 An indecomposable injective has simple socle: embed its finite-length socle into the direct sum of the injective hulls from [F3], extend that embedding to the whole object by injectivity of the target, and note that the kernel is zero because any nonzero finite-length submodule meets the socle. Injectivity of the source splits the embedding; indecomposability and uniqueness of injective hulls then give one hull. Every simple submodule of a Verma-filtered object embeds into some flag factor (take the first flag position it meets), so [F2] forces its label to be $a$. Hence every projective-injective indecomposable is the injective hull of $L(a)$, and is isomorphic to $P$. In particular the socle of $P$ is $L(a)$, once. [F2, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 For a finite $C$-module $N$, define $L(N)=P\otimes_CN$ by a finite presentation: the cokernel of the corresponding map between finite sums of $P$ exists in $\mathcal O$. Tensor-Hom adjunction gives $L\dashv V$; exactness of $V$ and $VP=C$ give $VL(N)\cong N$ by applying $V$ to that presentation. The counit $LVM\to M$ becomes an isomorphism under $V$, so its kernel and cokernel lie in $\ker V$. This supplies the equivalence $\mathcal O_\lambda/\ker V\simeq C\text{-mod}$: in the quotient every object is isomorphic to one of the $L(N)$, and adjunction identifies their quotient Hom maps with module maps. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Choose a linear functional $\omega:C\to\mathbb C$ nonzero on the top degree and zero on the other degrees. By [F1], $c\mapsto(d\mapsto\omega(cd))$ identifies $C$ with its vector-space dual as a $C$-module. For a finite $C$-module $N$, $\operatorname{Hom}_C(N,C^*)\cong N^*$ by evaluation at $1$, with inverse $\ell\mapsto(n\mapsto[c\mapsto\ell(cn)])$. Thus $C$ is injective among finite $C$-modules. The two contravariant functors $\operatorname{Hom}(-,P)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_C(V-,C)$ are exact. Their canonical comparison is an isomorphism on simples by step 1.1 and [F2]; it is nonzero at $L(a)$ because $P\twoheadrightarrow L(a)\hookrightarrow P$ is nonzero. Induction on finite length, using the two short exact Hom sequences, gives the comparison for all sources and target $P$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The unique maximal-weight Verma factor of $P$ lifts to an embedded $\Delta(\lambda)$ with Verma-filtered quotient. To see this, choose its position in a Verma flag. Earlier factors have no weights above $\lambda$ or at $\lambda$, so a lift of its highest vector is killed by $\mathfrak n^+$. The universal Verma map is injective because its composite to that flag factor is the identity. Its image splits that stage, and quotienting the full flag removes just this factor. Every Verma is annihilated by $C_+$ under the central action [F1], so $\Delta(\lambda)\subseteq K:=\{v\in P:C_+v=0\}$. If $K/\Delta(\lambda)\ne0$, it is a submodule of the Verma-filtered quotient; its socle contains $L(a)$ by the flag argument in step 1.1. Exactness of $V$ would give $\dim VK\ge2$, since $\dim V\Delta(\lambda)=1$. But inclusion into $P$ identifies $VK$ with a subspace of the one-dimensional socle of $VP=C$: every map $P\to K$ has image killed by $C_+$. This is impossible. Thus $K=\Delta(\lambda)$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The comparison for target $P$ in step 2.1 intertwines the central action. Its subspace of maps annihilated by $C_+$ is exactly $\operatorname{Hom}(M,K)$ on the category-$\mathcal O$ side and $\operatorname{Hom}_C(VM,\operatorname{soc}C)$ on the module side. Step 2.2 and exactness identify these subspaces with $\operatorname{Hom}(M,\Delta(\lambda))$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_C(VM,V\Delta(\lambda))$. This proves the comparison for the dominant Verma without an invalid induction for merely left-exact functors. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 A wall word $F$ and its adjoint word $G$ send $P$ to projective-injective objects; by step 1.1 these are finite sums of $P$. Therefore $VX=0$ implies $VFX=\operatorname{Hom}(GP,X)=0$, and likewise for $G$. The exact adjunction descends to the Serre quotient: its unit and counit induce maps there, and the triangle identities descend as equalities. Under step 1.2 it is an adjunction between the induced $C$-module functors. Combining the original adjunction, step 3.1 and this descended adjunction gives the canonical chain $\operatorname{Hom}(M,F\Delta(\lambda))\cong\operatorname{Hom}(GM,\Delta(\lambda))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_C(VGM,V\Delta(\lambda))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_C(VM,VF\Delta(\lambda))$. [F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra]

5.1 Every projective is a summand of a finite sum of the wall words in [F4]. The natural comparison in step 4.1 respects the summand idempotents, so restriction gives the required isomorphism for every projective target $Q$ and every source $M$. Step 1.2 also proves faithfulness on the quotient. No claim of full faithfulness on all original objects is made. [F4, step 1.2, step 4.1] ∎

items.title: Wall-crossing under the Soergel functor is tensoring with the coinvariant bimodule
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a regular integral block and simple reflection
$s$, with $C=\operatorname{End}(P(w_0\cdot\lambda))$, there is a natural
isomorphism of functors to left $C$-modules
$$V\theta_s\cong C\otimes_{C^s}V.$$
Equivalently the functor is tensoring by the $(C,C)$-bimodule
$C\otimes_{C^s}C$, with left action on the first factor and right action on the
second. In type A over $\mathbb C$, its polynomial lift is tensoring on the
left by $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$; read up to the auxiliary suspension
normalisation fixed by the rank-one case, the right origin reduction of $B_s$
is the two-dimensional module of centered degrees $-1,1$, for $M=S$ the
coinvariant reduction satisfies
$B_s\otimes_SC\cong(C\otimes_{C^s}C)(1)$ in the same normalisation, and
$B_s\otimes_S\mathbb C$ itself is not the bimodule $C\otimes_{C^s}C$: the
former has vector-space dimension two, whereas the latter has dimension
$2|W|$. Forgetting the grading gives the displayed category-$\mathcal O$
formula, and no grading on arbitrary category-$\mathcal O$ objects is asserted.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; translated endomorphism actions and descended adjunctions, as in Soergel §2.4, Theorem 10 and Corollary 1.

1.1 Set $V_
u=\operatorname{Hom}(P_
u,-)$. It is exact and induces the singular quotient equivalence with finite $C^s$-modules by the same finite-presentation argument $P_
u\otimes_{C^s}-\dashv V_
u$ used in [F2]. Adjunction and the chosen identification in [F1] give $V_
u T_{\mathrm{on}}M\cong\operatorname{Hom}(T_{\mathrm{out}}P_
u,M)\cong V_\lambda M$. Precomposition by an element of $\operatorname{End}(P_
u)$ becomes precomposition by its translated endomorphism of $P_\lambda$, which is the inclusion $C^s\hookrightarrow C$ in [F1]. Hence this is an isomorphism of $C^s$-module functors $V_
u T_{\mathrm{on}}\cong\operatorname{Res}_{C^s}^C V_\lambda$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Both translations preserve the kernels of these quotient functors. For $T_{\mathrm{on}}$ this follows from step 1.1. For the return functor, $T_{\mathrm{on}}P_\lambda$ is projective-injective by [F3]. In the singular block its indecomposable summands are copies of $P_
u$: the unique simple Verma is the antidominant one (the same integral Verma embedding argument as in the regular block), every projective has a Verma flag, so every simple submodule of a projective has this label; an indecomposable injective is its injective hull, by the finite-socle argument in the Struktursatz proof [F2]. Thus $T_{\mathrm{on}}P_\lambda=P_
u^{\oplus m}$ for some finite $m$. If $V_
u N=0$, adjunction gives $V_\lambda T_{\mathrm{out}}N=\operatorname{Hom}(T_{\mathrm{on}}P_\lambda,N)=0$. The exact adjunction $T_{\mathrm{out}}\dashv T_{\mathrm{on}}$ therefore descends to the two Serre quotients: the unit, counit and their triangle identities descend. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Under the quotient equivalences, the onto-wall functor is restriction by step 1.1. Its descended left adjoint is uniquely isomorphic to extension of scalars $C\otimes_{C^s}-$: the elementary adjunction sends a map $C\otimes_{C^s}N	o M$ to $n\mapsto f(1\otimes n)$, with inverse $c\otimes n\mapsto c g(n)$. Thus $V_\lambda T_{\mathrm{out}}\cong C\otimes_{C^s}V_
u$ as module functors, with the $C$-action established by adjunction rather than just a vector-space dimension count. Composing with step 1.1 proves $V	heta_s\cong C\otimes_{C^s}V$, equivalently tensoring by the $(C,C)$-bimodule $C\otimes_{C^s}C$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $J$ be the ideal of $S^s$ generated by $S^W_+$. Then $I=SJ=J\oplus\alpha J$ under [F4], so $C=(S^s/J)\oplus\alpha(S^s/J)$ and averaging over $s$ identifies $S^s/J=C^s$. Thus $C$ is free over $C^s$ with generators in degrees $0,2$. The natural tensor map $S\otimes_{S^s}C	o C\otimes_{C^s}C$ is an isomorphism: its left $I$ acts as zero since the generators $S^W_+$ balance to zero on the right; factoring the left quotient and the image of $S^s$ therefore gives inverse maps on pure tensors. Hence $B_s\otimes_SC\cong(C\otimes_{C^s}C)(1)$ as graded bimodules. As left $C$-modules this is $C(1)\oplus C(-1)$, not $C(1)\oplus C(3)$, because a degree-two generator contributes the external shift $(-2)$. Its dimension is $2|W|$, whereas $B_s\otimes_S\mathbb C$ has the two centered degrees $-1,1$. This proves the polynomial comparison and the dimension distinction without imposing any grading on category $\mathcal O$. [F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
